title: INDEPENDENT REGIONS
summary_en: Drive the evolution of the world into INDEPENDENT REGIONS: each region has its own natural geographic boundaries, its own economy, practices self-governance and self-administration, holds a respective seat in the world government, and is not subject to the intermediate authority of larger nation-states. A metropolitan region can only reach a state of equilibrium when it is small enough and sufficiently autonomous to operate as an independent cultural sphere.

numbers_en.k: Upper and lower population limits for each INDEPENDENT REGION
Total number of global regions divided according to this population size (caption from the original book's illustration)

Magnitude of interpersonal links required to maintain communication in a community of N people — once this threshold is exceeded, the process of bureaucracy overwhelming human beings will be triggered

references: J. B. S. Haldane, “On Being the Right Size,” in The World of Mathematics, Vol. II, J. R. Newman, ed. New York: Simon and Schuster, 1956, pp. 962–67.

title: THE DISTRIBUTION OF TOWNS
summary_en: Encourage the "birth and death process" of towns within a region, so that two objectives are gradually achieved: (1) the population is evenly distributed across different size hierarchies; (2) towns of each size hierarchy are spread uniformly across the region rather than clustered together. If the population is overly skewed toward small villages, modern civilization cannot emerge; if it is overly skewed toward large cities, land will fall into disrepair and abandonment due to lack of proper stewardship.

numbers_en.k: Ratio of the number of towns across all size hierarchies
Population of towns corresponding to the four hierarchies
Spacing between million-population cities
Spacing between 100,000-population towns
Spacing between 10,000-population towns
Spacing between 1,000-population towns and villages

references: Brian Berry and William Garrison, “Alternate Explanations of Urban Rank-Size Relationships,” Annals of the Association of American Geographers, Vol. 48, No. 1, March 1958, pp. 83–91.
“Urban Growth Policies in Six European Countries,” Urban Growth Policy Study Group, Office of International Affairs, HUD, Washington, D.C., 1972.

title: CITY COUNTRY FINGERS
summary_en: Maintain interlaced finger belts of farmland and urban land, even in central metropolitan areas. Under the CITY COUNTRY FINGERS framework, the width of any urban finger belt shall not exceed 1 mile, and the width of any farmland finger belt shall not be less than 1 mile. People only feel comfortable when they have constant access to the countryside, pastoral landscapes and wild flora and fauna, while cities are only vibrant when supporting high-density interaction between people and jobs; the two elements must interlock, rather than one being swallowed by the other.

numbers_en.k: Maximum width of urban finger belts
Minimum width of farmland finger belts
Maximum walking time for every person to reach the countryside — the 1-mile upper limit of urban belts is derived from this standard
Size threshold below which 90% of farms fall — the lower limit of farmland belts is set based on this metric
Decline in the proportion of the population preferring to live in cities over the short 6-year period from 1966 to 1972
Share of Americans living in rural areas a century ago, compared with the share of the population living in cities today

references: George Gallup, “Most don’t want to live in a city,” San Francisco Chronicle, December 18, 1972, p. 12.
H. H. Iltis, P. Andres, and O. L. Loucks, in Population Resources Environment: Issues in Human Ecology, P. R. Ehrlich and A. H. Ehrlich, San Francisco: Freeman.
Gerald D. Adams, “The Open Space Explosion,” Cry California, Fall 1970, pp. 27–32.
Leon H. Keyserling, Agriculture and the Public Interest, Conference on Economic Progress, Washington, D.C., February 1965.

title: AGRICULTURAL VALLEYS
summary_en: Retain all AGRICULTURAL VALLEYS as farmland, and protect this land from any development that would damage or permanently seal off its unique soil fertility. Even if the valleys are not currently under cultivation, they shall still be protected, and reserved for farms, parks and wilderness areas.

numbers_en.k: The fertility of alluvial soil is concentrated on the valley floor, which is a non-renewable limited resource
Settlements shall be sited on slopes and uplands, to free up the flat, fertile valley floor

references: Ian McHarg, Design With Nature, New York: Natural History Press, 1969.
Wallace-McHarg Associates, Philadelphia, 1963.

title: LACE OF COUNTRY STREETS
summary_en: At the urban-rural interface, country streets are spaced at least 1 mile apart to enclose blocks of open countryside and farmland no smaller than 1 square mile, forming the LACE OF COUNTRY STREETS configuration. Residences are built along these roads in a single row, with each lot covering a minimum of 0.5 acres, so that the full 1-square-mile expanse of open fields sits directly behind each home. While many people wish to live in a rural environment while staying in close proximity to large cities, it is geometrically impossible to site thousands of small farms all within a few minutes’ drive of a major urban core.

numbers_en.k: Minimum spacing between adjacent country streets
Minimum area of countryside/farmland blocks enclosed by streets
Residences are arranged in only one row along roads, with no inward sprawl into the field block
Minimum residential lot area per household
Reference capacity of one such country street network

references: Land Use and Built Form Studies, Cambridge, England, 1968.

title: COUNTRY TOWNS
summary_en: Protect existing COUNTRY TOWNS, and encourage the growth of new self-sufficient towns with a population between 500 and 10,000, fully surrounded by open countryside, and located at least 10 miles away from adjacent towns. The shared priority across the entire region is to secure capital for local industry development in each town, so that these settlements will not become bedroom communities where residents commute to other locations for work, but genuine towns capable of supporting a complete, full-functioning way of life.

numbers_en.k: Population range of a self-sufficient COUNTRY TOWN
Minimum distance from adjacent towns
Requirement that each town be fully surrounded by open countryside and not connected to other built-up areas
U.S. rural population that migrated to urban areas over the past 30 years

references: Joe Evins 在美国众议院提出的相关法案,见 Congressional Record — House, October 3, 1967.

title: THE COUNTRYSIDE
summary_en: Define all farms as parks with guaranteed public access, and convert all regional parks into fully operational working farms. A steward system is established across individuals, families and cooperatives, where each stewardship responsibility corresponds to a distinct section of THE COUNTRYSIDE. Stewards obtain land leases, with full autonomy to manage the land (including small farms, woodlands, marshes and deserts) and set rules for its use, while the public may freely visit, hike, picnic, explore and go boating on the land as long as they comply with these rules.

numbers_en.k: All farms grant the public legal right of access
All regional parks must be operational productive land
Each steward (individual/household/cooperative) is assigned one designated section of THE COUNTRYSIDE

references: Aldo Leopold, A Sand County Almanac, New York: Oxford University Press, 1949.
The Ecologist, England: Penguin, 1972, p. 41.
John L. Creech, “Japan — Like a National Park,” Yearbook of Agriculture 1963, U. S. Department of Agriculture, pp. 525–28.

title: MOSAIC OF SUBCULTURES
summary_en: Make every possible effort to enrich the city's culture and subcultures, and decompose the city as thoroughly as possible into a large MOSAIC OF SUBCULTURES composed of many small, distinct subcultures. Each subculture has its own spatial territory, and is entitled to create its own unique lifestyle. At the same time, it is necessary to ensure these subcultures are sufficiently small, so that every person can conveniently access the full range of diverse lifestyles in their immediate surroundings.

numbers_en.k: Upper size limit of each subculture territory — small enough for people to access multiple lifestyles in adjacent areas
Each subculture requires its own distinct spatial territory, rather than being mixed indistinctly with one another
Relevant spatial scale reference discussed in the source book

references: Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania: University of Pittsburgh, February 1969.

title: SCATTERED WORK
summary_en: Use zoning regulations, neighborhood planning, tax incentives, and all available applicable measures to disperse workplaces across the entire city under the SCATTERED WORK framework. Large contiguous areas dedicated solely to work with no surrounding family residential life are prohibited, while large contiguous areas dedicated solely to residential life with no adjacent workplaces are also prohibited.

numbers_en.k: Neither single-use employment zones nor single-use residential zones are permitted — prohibitions are enforced in both directions
Reference commute time discussed in the book

references: George Woodcock, Anarchism: A History of Libertarian Ideas and Movements.
Raymond Vernon, Metropolis 1985, Chapter 7: External Economies.
Lewis Mumford, Sticks and Stones, New York, 1924, p. 216.
Small Sellers and Large Buyers in American Industry, Business Research Center, College of Business Administration, Syracuse University.

title: MAGIC OF THE CITY
summary_en: Make the MAGIC OF THE CITY easily accessible to every person across the entire metropolitan area. This is implemented via regional collective policies that impose strict constraints on the growth of city centers, so that the population served by any individual city center does not exceed 300,000. With this population base, the distance between different city centers ranges from 2 to 9 miles.

numbers_en.k: Upper limit of the population served by any single city center
Distance between city centers derived from this population baseline
A structure that does not have one giant center, but several moderately sized centers located a short distance from one another

references: P. K. Hatt and A. J. Reiss, eds., Cities and Society, New York: The Free Press, 1967, pp. 759–72.
Geography of Market Centers and Retail Distribution, New Jersey: Prentice-Hall, 1967, p. 47.
American Institute of Planners Journal, May 1965, pp. 134–43.

title: LOCAL TRANSPORT AREAS
summary_en: Divide urban areas into individual LOCAL TRANSPORT AREAS, each spanning 1 to 2 miles and surrounded by a full ring road. Only minor local routes for pedestrians, cyclists, equestrians, and local vehicles are constructed within each area; arterial roads are designed to allow cars and trucks to enter and exit the ring road conveniently, but laid out to make through travel inside the area both slow and inconvenient. The value and power of motor vehicles have proven so significant that they must be constrained through physical urban form, rather than relying on discouragement measures.

numbers_en.k: Span of each LOCAL TRANSPORT AREA
Each area is completely enclosed by a peripheral ring road
Arterial roads facilitate convenient access to and from the ring road, while through movement within the area must be slow and inconvenient

title: COMMUNITY OF 7000
summary_en: Devolve authority from municipal governments to place local control in the hands of communities with a population of 5,000 to 10,000, the scale corresponding to the COMMUNITY OF 7000. These communities shall be demarcated as far as possible using natural geographic boundaries and historical boundaries. Each community is vested with the power to initiate, decide on, and execute matters closely tied to its local interests, covering land use, housing, maintenance, streets, parks, policing, education, welfare, and neighborhood services. Only when self-governing units are sufficiently small can residents exert real, tangible influence on local politics.

numbers_en.k: Population range of one self-governing community
Community boundaries shall be derived from existing traces such as rivers, ridgelines, old walls, rather than regularized demarcation lines

numbers_en.v: Land use, housing, maintenance, streets, parks, policing, education, welfare, neighborhood services
numbers_en.k: Nine self-governance powers

references: Milton Kotler, Neighborhood Foundations, Memorandum #24: “Neighborhood corporations and the reorganization of city government.”
Committee on Government Operations, U.S. Senate, 89th Congress, Second Session, Part 9, December 1966.
Blueprint for Survival, Penguin Books, 1972, pp. 50–55.

title: SUBCULTURE BOUNDARY
summary_en: Separate adjacent subcultures with a zone at least 200 feet wide, defined as SUBCULTURE BOUNDARY. This boundary can be natural, including wilderness, farmland and water bodies, or man-made, including railways, major arterial roads, parks, schools, and even portions of residential areas. At the interface seam where the two subcultures meet, construct shared gathering spaces and shared functions that simultaneously engage communities on both sides.

numbers_en.k: Minimum width of the zone separating adjacent subcultures
Dual function of the boundary: separating the two subcultures from each other, and hosting shared functions at the interface seam
Wilderness, farmland, water bodies, railways, major arterial roads, parks, and schools can all serve as the boundary

references: Planning and the Purchase Decision: Why People Buy in Planned Communities, University of California.
Ernst Mayr, Animal Species and Evolution, Cambridge, 1963, Chapter 18: “The Ecology of Speciation.”

title: IDENTIFIABLE NEIGHBORHOOD
summary_en: Help people define the IDENTIFIABLE NEIGHBORHOOD they reside in, which is no more than 300 yards square and has a resident population not exceeding 400 to 500 people. In existing cities, encourage local groups to self-organize to form such neighborhoods, and grant them a certain degree of autonomy in taxation and land control. Major arterial roads are excluded from the interior of these neighborhoods. Current development patterns are destroying neighborhoods.

numbers_en.k: Maximum square dimension of the identifiable neighborhood
Maximum resident population cap of one identifiable neighborhood

numbers_en.v: Major arterial roads are sited outside neighborhoods
numbers_en.k: Major arterial roads must be routed between neighborhoods, and shall never pass through the interior of a neighborhood

references: Anthony Wallace, Housing and Social Structure, Philadelphia Housing Authority.
Mary W. Herman, “Comparative Studies of Identification Areas in Philadelphia,” City of Philadelphia.
Donald Appleyard and Mark Lintell, “Environmental Quality of City Streets,” Center for Planning and Development Research, Berkeley.

title: NEIGHBORHOOD BOUNDARY
summary_en: Encourage the formation of a NEIGHBORHOOD BOUNDARY around each neighborhood to separate it from adjacent neighborhoods. This is implemented by closing selected streets and restricting access, cutting the total number of regular streets by at least half. Install gateways at points where restricted access routes cross the boundary, and make the boundary zone sufficiently wide to accommodate public functions and gathering spaces shared by multiple neighborhoods. The book uses the analogy that the boundary is to a neighborhood what the cell wall is to a cell.

numbers_en.k: The number of streets leading to the neighborhood is reduced by at least half, with the remaining closed off to form dead-end streets
Set up gateways at locations where the retained access routes cross the boundary
The boundary zone must be wide enough to accommodate public functions shared by multiple neighborhoods

title: WEB OF PUBLIC TRANSPORTATION
summary_en: Treat transfer points as the primary element and routes as the secondary element. Create incentives for all different public transport modes — aircraft, helicopters, ferries, ships, trains, rapid transit, buses, minibuses, cable cars, escalators, moving walkways, elevators — to plan routes that connect these transfer points, with the expectation that gradually, many different types of routes will converge at each transfer point. Cede control of transfer points to local communities.

numbers_en.k: Take transfer points as the primary design object, with routes subordinate to transfer points
The goal is to have an increasing number of different route types meet at each transfer point
Relevant walking transfer scale discussed in the book

references: Colin Ward, “The Organization of Anarchy,” in Patterns of Anarchy, Leonard I. Krimerman and Lewis Perry, eds.

title: RING ROADS
summary_en: Arrange expressways (motorways and other major arterial roads) per the following three provisions: (1) At least one expressway is tangent to each local traffic zone; (2) Each local traffic zone has at least one side not enclosed by expressways, opening directly to the open countryside; (3) Roads are consistently sunken below grade, or screened along their alignment by earthen berms, earth cover, or industrial buildings, to protect adjacent neighborhoods from traffic noise.

numbers_en.k: At least one expressway is tangent to each local traffic zone (rather than traversing the zone)
Each zone has at least one side not enclosed by expressways, opening directly to the open countryside
Roads are sunken or screened along the route by earthen berms, earth cover, and industrial buildings to block noise

title: NETWORK OF LEARNING
summary_en: Reject the lockstep model of compulsory education confined to fixed premises, and gradually decentralize the learning process to enrich it through interactions with numerous locations and people across the entire city. These resources include workshops, teachers who work from home or travel around the city, professionals willing to take young people as assistants, older children tutoring younger children, museums, traveling youth groups, academic seminars, industrial workshops, and elderly residents. All of these diverse actors and spaces are regarded as constituent parts of the NETWORK OF LEARNING.

numbers_en.k: Learning is dispersed across many sites throughout the city, rather than being concentrated in schools
Teachers, professionals, elderly residents, and older children all act as learning nodes in the network
There is no 'central school' — every point is only an ordinary node within the network

references: George Dennison, The Lives of Children, New York: Vintage Books, 1969, p. 3.
Ivan Illich, Deschooling Society

title: WEB OF SHOPPING
summary_en: When selecting a site for any retail store, a standardized four-step procedure is followed: (1) Mark all other stores offering the same type of service on a map; (2) Plot the locations and density of potential customers; (3) Site the new store at the location with the largest gap in the WEB OF SHOPPING that is covered by potential customers; (4) Within that identified gap, position the store as close as possible to the largest agglomeration of different types of non-competing stores. The core guiding tension of this site selection logic is to maintain appropriate distance from same-category stores while staying proximate to different-category stores.

numbers_en.k: Located at the largest gap in the WEB OF SHOPPING of same-category stores to avoid competition
Within the identified gap, position as close as possible to the largest agglomeration of different-category stores to share customer flow
Mark same-category stores → Mark customers → Identify the largest gap → Approach different-category store agglomeration

references: S. Angel and F. Loetterle, “Computer Simulation of Market Location in an Urban Area,” CES files.
Brian Berry, Geography of Market Centers and Retail Distribution, Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey: Prentice-Hall, 1967.

title: MINI-BUSES
summary_en: Establish a taxi-style public transit system operated by MINI-BUSES: each vehicle carries a maximum of 6 passengers, is dispatched via radio, supports telephone booking, and provides point-to-point service tailored to passenger demand, with a dedicated computer system that ensures minimal detours and the shortest possible wait times. Dedicated stops are set up for MINI-BUSES at 600-foot intervals in all directions, with a telephone installed at each stop that can directly call for a MINI-BUS.

numbers_en.k: Passenger capacity limit per MINI-BUS — between that of a taxi and a conventional public transit bus
Stop spacing in all directions, with a telephone installed at each stop for vehicle hailing
On-demand point-to-point service enabled by telephone hailing and radio dispatch
Order of magnitude of the minimum wait time guaranteed by computerized dispatch

references: W. G. Atkinson et al., Regina Telebus Study: Operations Report and Financial Report, June 1974.
Sumner Myers, “Turning Transit Subsidies into ‘Compensatory Transportation,’” City, Vol. 6, No. 4.

title: FOUR-STORY LIMIT
summary_en: In any urban area, no matter how dense, most buildings are kept at four stories or below per the FOUR-STORY LIMIT. A small number of buildings may exceed this threshold, but they must never be residential structures. High-rise buildings offer no real benefits other than generating speculative profits for banks and landowners: they are not cheaper to develop, do not help create open space, and instead damage townscapes, erode social life, and contribute to higher crime rates.

numbers_en.k: Height upper limit for the majority of buildings
Very small number of buildings permitted to exceed the limit, which must never be for human habitation
High-rises are not cheaper, do not conserve land, and instead harm social life

references: “Families in Flats,” British Medical Journal, November 18, 1967, pp. 382–86.
D. V. Canter and others 关于高层居住社会影响的研究。

title: NINE PER CENT PARKING
summary_en: Within any given area, the total land dedicated to parking may not exceed 9%. To prevent contiguous parking concentrations from forming large swathes of neglected wasteland, towns and communities must subdivide their territory into NINE PER CENT PARKING districts, each with a maximum area of no more than 10 acres. The same 9% parking land cap rule is implemented uniformly within each of these districts.

numbers_en.k: Upper limit of the proportion of land allocated to parking in any given area
Upper limit of the area of each NINE PER CENT PARKING district, to prevent clustered contiguous parking development
Counter reference: Proportion of land allocated to automobiles in Downtown Los Angeles

title: PARALLEL ROADS
summary_en: Within a local traffic zone, no intersecting arterial roads are constructed at all; instead, a system of parallel, alternating one-way roads directs traffic flow to the ring road. In existing towns, this structure is established incrementally by gradually converting major streets to one-way operation and closing cross streets. Parallel roads are spaced at least 100 yards apart (to reserve space for the intervening neighborhood) and no more than 300 to 400 yards apart.

numbers_en.k: No intersecting arterial roads are built within the local traffic zone
A set of parallel one-way roads with alternating directions is used as the replacement
Spacing between parallel roads: the lower bound reserves space for neighborhoods, the upper bound ensures accessibility

references: C. Alexander, “The Pattern of Streets,” AIP Journal, September 1966.
G. F. Newell, “The Effect of Left Turns on the Capacity of a Traffic Intersection,” Quarterly of Applied Mathematics.

title: SACRED SITES
summary_en: Regardless of the size of SACRED SITES, and whether they are situated in town centers, within neighborhoods, or in the most remote rural areas, they shall be afforded absolute statutory protection, so that the roots anchoring us to the visible built and natural environment and to the past remain inviolable. Informal community experiments confirm that people share a surprisingly high degree of consensus on which sites genuinely hold the public’s connections to the land and to the past.

numbers_en.k: All SACRED SITES are subject to absolute statutory protection regardless of their size and location
People show remarkably consistent judgments of which locations qualify as SACRED SITES
SACRED SITES are scattered across all parts of the daily spatial fabric, rather than being concentrated or enclosed as tourist attractions

title: ACCESS TO WATER
summary_en: When natural water bodies are close to human settlements, treat them with utmost respect. Always reserve a continuous strip of public land immediately adjacent to the water's edge; high-density settlements are only permitted to extend all the way to the waterfront at a very small number of widely spaced locations. Two undesirable outcomes must both be avoided: (1) roads, highways and industrial uses destroy the waterfront, rendering it dirty or dangerous and nearly inaccessible, and (2) the waterfront is protected but falls into exclusive private ownership.

numbers_en.k: Permanently reserve an unbroken public land strip immediately adjacent to the water's edge
High-density settlements extend to the waterfront only at a small number of widely spaced locations
(1) Roads and industrial uses damage the waterfront, (2) The waterfront is enclosed and occupied by private interests

title: LIFE CYCLE
summary_en: Ensure a complete and balanced LIFE CYCLE is represented in every community. This means (1) each community includes people across all life stages, from infants to the oldest old, and is fully equipped with the full range of venues required for each of these stages; (2) the community is also furnished with the transition venues that most distinctly mark a person’s progression from one life stage to the next. To live fully in each of the seven age stages, every age must be clearly marked by the community as a distinct, well-defined period of time, which can only be realized when the rituals marking these transitions are formally observed through public celebrations.

numbers_en.k: Shakespeare's 'Seven Ages of Man': infant, juvenile, youth, family-forming adult, prime-age adult, senior, advanced elderly
Each community must have residents across all age groups, rather than consisting of only a single generation
Equip communities with ceremonial spaces that mark the crossing between life stages, so that every life transition is formally marked by celebratory events

references: Shakespeare, As You Like It, II.vii(「人生七阶」独白).
Erik Erikson 关于生命周期八阶段的心理社会发展理论。

title: MEN AND WOMEN
summary_en: Ensure that every component of the environment — every building, every open space, every neighborhood, every work community — is shaped by the fusion of the two inherent instincts of MEN AND WOMEN. Across every scale and every project, from kitchens to steel mills, this balance of masculine and feminine qualities must be maintained. Since no aspect of life is purely masculine or purely feminine, a world that pushes gender separation to extremes will distort reality, and perpetuate and solidify this distortion permanently.

numbers_en.k: The two instincts are intertwined in the same site, rather than split into a binary dichotomy
This balance must be addressed for every project, ranging from kitchens to steel mills
No aspect of life is entirely masculine or entirely feminine

title: ECCENTRIC NUCLEUS
summary_en: Encourage density growth and accumulation to form a distinct "peak-valley" pattern in accordance with the following rules: (1) Regard towns as collections of multiple 7,000-person communities, whose square dimensions range from a quarter mile to two miles based on their overall density; (2) Identify the point on each community's boundary that lies closest to the nearest large city — this point is the density peak and the ECCENTRIC NUCLEUS of the community. The core principle is that the nucleus is not situated at the center of the community, but on the edge facing the adjacent large city.

numbers_en.k: Nucleus located on the side of the community boundary closest to the large city, not at the center
Square dimension of 7,000-person communities determined by overall density
Density forms distinct peaks and valleys rather than spreading out uniformly

references: T. Brennan, Midland City, London: Dobson, 1948.

title: DENSITY RINGS
summary_en: Once the core of a community is clearly located, define successive outward rings of residential density that decrease incrementally away from this core. If no other arrangement is feasible, select corresponding values from the established density table, but the better practice is to play the "DENSITY RINGS game" to derive these density values from the intuitive perceptions of the people who will reside in the community. Note that the core is offset (see Eccentric Core), so the density gradient decreases outward from this offset core, rather than radiating from a concentric bullseye at the exact center of the site layout.

numbers_en.v: Dense near the core, sparse at the periphery
numbers_en.k: Density decreases in successive rings extending outward from the core
The density gradient takes the offset core as its starting point, not a centered set of concentric circles
The optimal practice is to derive the density of each ring from the intuitive preferences of future residents, rather than rigidly applying pre-set tabulated values

title: ACTIVITY NODES
summary_en: Create ACTIVITY NODES across the entire community, spaced approximately 300 yards apart. First identify existing sites in the community where movement naturally tends to cluster, then adjust the layout of the community path network to route as many paths as possible through these sites, turning each site into a node within the path network. Then, develop a small public square at the center of each node, enclosed by a set of supporting community facilities.

numbers_en.k: Spacing between adjacent ACTIVITY NODES
Numerous nodes spread across the entire community, rather than a single central square
Adjust the road network to direct as many routes as possible through these natural gathering points

references: Ray Bradbury, “The girls walk this way; the boys walk that way …,” West(Los Angeles Times Magazine).

title: PROMENADE
summary_en: Encourage the gradual formation of a PROMENADE at the center of each neighborhood, which connects major activity nodes and is centrally laid out to ensure every point in the neighborhood is within a 10-minute walking distance. Position one primary attractor at each of its two ends to maintain continuous back-and-forth pedestrian flow. This is the paseo, passeggiata commonly seen in small towns across Italy, Spain, Mexico, Greece and other regions: the evening stroll, where people come to walk, meet friends, and observe passersby.

numbers_en.k: Maximum walking time from any point in the neighborhood to the promenade
One attractor placed at each end to sustain back-and-forth pedestrian flow
The promenade is a linear pedestrian street where people walk back and forth along it, rather than staying in a plaza

title: SHOPPING STREET
summary_en: Encourage local shopping centers to develop into the form of a short SHOPPING STREET, oriented at a right angle to the main road with access openings leading from the main road, and parking lots arranged behind the storefronts. This layout allows vehicles to pull directly off the main road without impairing the function of the SHOPPING STREET itself.

numbers_en.k: The short shopping street is oriented at a right angle to the main road, with access openings leading from the main road
Parking lots are sited behind storefronts, allowing vehicles to pull directly off the main road
Vehicles are not permitted to enter the pedestrian street, and pedestrians exclusively use the central street space

title: NIGHT LIFE
summary_en: Integrate after-hours shops, entertainment venues and service facilities, together with hotels, bars and all-night restaurants, to form NIGHT LIFE centers: bright, safe, vibrant destinations that attract all people venturing out at night to the same handful of locations across the city, thereby increasing the intensity of nighttime pedestrian activity. These nighttime centers are encouraged to be evenly distributed across the entire urban area.

numbers_en.k: Interweave after-hours shops, entertainment venues, hotels, bars and all-night restaurants
Multiple NIGHT LIFE centers spread evenly across the city, rather than a single large central hub
Gather nighttime pedestrians at several shared locations to boost nighttime walking intensity and safety

title: INTERCHANGE
summary_en: At every interchange point across the transit network, adhere to the following principles: (1) Surround the interchange with workplace and residential typologies that have particularly high demand for public transit access; (2) Preserve the continuity of the pedestrian network both inside and outside the interchange station, sustain this continuity via integrated small shops and newsstands, and locate all parking facilities to one side of the site; (3) Keep transfer distances between different transport modes within 300 feet whenever feasible, with a non-negotiable absolute upper limit of 600 feet.

numbers_en.k: Transfer distance between different transport modes to be controlled within this range as much as possible
Absolute upper limit of transfer distance
Surround the interchange with workplaces and residences that have particularly high public transit demand

title: HOUSEHOLD MIX
summary_en: Encourage every neighborhood and every residential cluster to develop toward HOUSEHOLD MIX, so that one-person households, couples, families with children, and co-living groups live adjacent to one another. People require both the support and validation from individuals at different life cycle stages, and the support from peers at the same life stage. However, demands that drive household segregation often outweigh the demand for HOUSEHOLD MIX.

numbers_en.k: One-person households, couples, families with children, and co-living groups live in proximity to one another
HOUSEHOLD MIX takes place inside each residential cluster, rather than implementing separate zoning by unit type
People need support from peers at the same life stage, as well as validation from people at different life stages

title: DEGREES OF PUBLICNESS
summary_en: Explicitly classify dwellings into three distinct categories: those located in quiet, secluded locations, those situated on busy streets, and the more or less intermediate types between the two extremes. Secluded dwellings are placed along winding paths and physically concealed from public view, publicly oriented dwellings are sited on busy streets with non-stop all-day pedestrian flow, with the building itself relatively exposed to passersby, while intermediate dwellings are arranged at the midpoint between the two settings. This arrangement allows people to select the DEGREES OF PUBLICNESS of their housing that aligns with their personal temperament.

numbers_en.v: Three tiers of DEGREES OF PUBLICNESS
numbers_en.k: Secluded / Intermediate / Street-facing exposed
Approximate distribution ratio of the three tiers (secluded / intermediate / street-facing)
Relevant neighborhood scale reference discussed in the book

title: HOUSE CLUSTER
summary_en: Arrange residential units into roughly sized yet clearly identifiable HOUSE CLUSTERs of 8 to 12 units each, organized around a shared common open space and pedestrian path. These HOUSE CLUSTERs are laid out to allow any person to traverse the area without feeling that they are trespassing. In existing single-family detached home neighborhoods, this pattern is implemented via gradual relaxation of zoning regulations, permitting incremental weaving of HOUSE CLUSTER configurations into the existing street grid.

numbers_en.k: Number of units per HOUSE CLUSTER: large enough to support shared communal life, small enough that all residents know one another
Each cluster is arranged around one shared common open space and pedestrian path
Any person may pass through the cluster without feeling they are trespassing

references: Martin Buber, A Believing Humanism: Gleanings, New York: Simon and Schuster, 1969, p. 94.

title: ROW HOUSES
summary_en: For ROW HOUSES, site the units along pedestrian paths running perpendicular to local streets and parking lots, giving each unit a long street frontage and shallow building depth. Once density exceeds 15 dwelling units per acre, it is nearly impossible to preserve single-family detached homes without destroying surrounding open space, as the remaining open area will be compressed into a thin, useless ring around the buildings. Apartments also cannot resolve the high-density problem, as they elevate residents away from the ground plane.

numbers_en.k: Layout along pedestrian paths oriented at right angles to streets and parking lots
Each unit is assigned a long street frontage and shallow building depth
Density above this threshold makes it impossible for single-family homes to retain usable open space

title: HOUSING HILL
summary_en: When the required net residential density exceeds 30 dwelling units per net acre, or the development program calls for 3 to 4 stories, implement the HOUSING HILL typology. These structures are designed as tiered south-facing receding terraces, connected by a full-height central south-facing grand stair that leads to a shared communal garden. Each household retains its own private terrace and direct south-facing daylight, achieving high density without the ground-detached, mutually isolated experience typical of conventional apartment blocks.

numbers_en.k: Density threshold triggering the HOUSING HILL typology
Condition for switching to HOUSING HILL when 3 to 4 stories of development are required
Tiered terraces recede southward, with every unit having a private terrace and south-facing sunlight

references: “Families in Flats,” British Medical Journal, November 1967, pp. 382–86.
J. F. Demers, “Park Hill Survey,” O.A.P., February 1966, p. 235.

title: OLD PEOPLE EVERYWHERE
summary_en: Construct housing for approximately 50 older adults in each neighborhood, arranged across three layers: ① a central core with a shared public kitchen and on-site care services; ② small cottages located close to the core; ③ small cottages situated further from the core, interspersed with other regular neighborhood residential units, and no more than 200 yards away from the core at any point. These 50 households collectively form a cohesive cluster with a distinct, clearly defined center, whose edges interlock and integrate with the surrounding ordinary neighborhood dwellings.

numbers_en.k: Number of older adults provided with dedicated housing per neighborhood
Central core (kitchen + care) / core-adjacent cottages / far-core mixed-in cottages
Maximum allowable distance from the outermost senior cottages to the central core

references: Time, August 3, 1970.

title: WORK COMMUNITY
summary_en: Foster or encourage the formation of WORK COMMUNITY, each of which is an assemblage of multiple smaller workplace clusters. Each of these clusters has its own dedicated courtyard, and all clusters are arranged around a larger shared public plaza or public yard that contains shops and lunch counters, with the entire WORK COMMUNITY accommodating no more than 10 to 20 workplaces. The fact that people invariably name their house or residential neighborhood when asked where they "live", and never mention the workplace where they spend most of their day, itself demonstrates how deeply work has been isolated.

numbers_en.k: Upper limit of total workplaces in one WORK COMMUNITY
Workplaces organized into small clusters each with its own small courtyard, sharing one public courtyard with stores and lunch counters
Work should not be isolated in office buildings, but support public life similar to that of a small village

title: INDUSTRIAL RIBBON
summary_en: Arrange industrial uses into 200 to 500-foot wide INDUSTRIAL RIBBONS that serve as boundaries between communities. These ribbons are divided into elongated blocks with areas ranging from 1 to 25 acres, and the edge of each ribbon is designated as a location where residents of nearby communities can benefit from derivatives of the hosted industrial activities. Industry does generate smoke, odors, noise and heavy truck traffic, so strict safeguards must be implemented to prevent the highest-impact heavy industrial uses from encroaching on residential areas, though industrial land does not need to be fully concealed.

numbers_en.k: Width of the industrial ribbon — sufficiently large to accommodate industrial uses without forming a segregation barrier wall
Area of the elongated blocks subdivided from the ribbon, with varying sizes across units
Industrial ribbon acts as the boundary between adjacent communities

references: Robert E. Boley, Industrial Districts Restudied: An Analysis of Characteristics.
A Pattern Language Which Generates Multi-Service Centers, Center for Environmental Structure, Berkeley.

title: UNIVERSITY AS A MARKETPLACE
summary_en: The core objective is to operate the university under the UNIVERSITY AS A MARKETPLACE framework. As a social conception, this means the university is open to people of all ages, with full-time, part-time, or single-course elective options, where any person can offer a course and any person can enroll in a course. Physically, this university marketplace has a central crossroads that accommodates all major buildings and administrative offices, with classrooms and laboratories spreading outward in a rippling pattern from this crossroads: starting with small structures along pedestrian streets, followed by progressively larger buildings further outward.

numbers_en.k: Open to people of all ages, with full-time, part-time, and single-course elective options all available

numbers_en.v: Universal access to teaching and learning
numbers_en.k: Any individual can offer a course, and any individual can select a course to take
Teaching sites are distributed along pedestrian streets like market stalls, rather than being concentrated in large buildings

title: LOCAL TOWN HALL
summary_en: To make political control over local affairs tangible, construct a small LOCAL TOWN HALL for every 7000-person community, and even for every neighborhood, and site it near the community's busiest intersection. The building contains three distinct components: an arena dedicated to public discussion, public service facilities arranged around this arena, and flexible spaces that can be leased to temporary community projects.

numbers_en.k: Every community (and even every neighborhood) has its own small LOCAL TOWN HALL
Sited near the community's busiest intersection, accessible to all passersby
Public discussion arena + surrounding public services + space leased to community projects

references: A Pattern Language Which Generates Multi-Service Centers, Center for Environmental Structure, Berkeley.

title: NECKLACE OF COMMUNITY PROJECTS
summary_en: Allow shop-sized spaces to be created around local municipal halls and other suitable community buildings, orient these storefronts toward a busy roadway, and lease them to temporary community groups at minimum rent for political work, experimental services, research and advocacy, with no ideological restrictions in place. A dynamic community self-governance process relies on the free operation of an endless stream of ad-hoc political and service groups, each afforded the opportunity to test its ideas before the public.

numbers_en.k: A series of small spaces at storefront scale arranged along a busy street
Leased to temporary community groups at minimum rent with extremely low access thresholds
Any grassroots group is eligible for tenancy, with no ideological stance screening

title: MARKET OF MANY SHOPS
summary_en: Reject modern supermarkets in favor of developing frequently sited MARKET OF MANY SHOPS, each composed of numerous independent, specialized small shops (cheese, meat, grain, fruit, etc.). The market’s built structure is kept to the absolute minimum, providing only a shared roof, columns that demarcate pedestrian aisles, and basic public services. Within this structural framework, individual shops may shape their own respective environments according to their unique preferences and operational needs.

numbers_en.k: A market consists of many specialized, independent small shops rather than a single supermarket
The market only provides a roof, columns, and basic services; the interior environment of each shop is created independently by its operator
Stall/aisle related dimension reference discussed in the source book

title: HEALTH CENTER
summary_en: Gradually develop a citywide network of small HEALTH CENTER facilities, with roughly one allocated for every community of 7,000 people. Each center can treat common minor physical and mental ailments for both children and adults, but is essentially structured around wellness and educational activities that help people maintain health, such as swimming and dancing. Hospitals are disease-focused: they are extremely costly, inconvenient due to excessive centralization, and reinforce the misconception that "health is the absence of illness".

numbers_en.k: Distribution density of small health centers
Organized around health-maintaining activities such as swimming and dancing, rather than centered on disease
Small, dispersed network that replaces expensive, centralized large hospitals

title: HOUSING IN BETWEEN
summary_en: Integrate housing into the urban fabric of all typically classified non-residential urban spaces that draw large crowds during daytime hours, including retail outlets, small-scale industrial facilities, schools, public service venues, and university precincts. Housing under the HOUSING IN BETWEEN framework can be arranged in contiguous rows, stacked in terraced "hill" configurations with retail on the ground level, or developed as standalone structures, as long as they are functionally mixed with adjacent uses to ensure the entire district remains inhabited. The individual, regular rhythm of property maintenance and repair is critical to the long-term health of every component of the community, as only on-site residents will tend to the neighborhood consistently day after day.

numbers_en.k: Integrate housing into the non-residential fabric between retail, industry, schools, universities and other similar land uses
Enable areas that are bustling during the day and vacant at night to have residents living on a 24-hour daily basis

numbers_en.v: Mixed use rather than single-use zoning
numbers_en.k: Mix housing with other functions instead of segregating them into exclusive single-function zones

title: LOOPED LOCAL ROADS
summary_en: Lay out local roads in the LOOPED LOCAL ROADS configuration. A loop is defined as any road segment that prevents through traffic with no destination on the segment from using it as a shortcut. No individual loop shall serve more than 50 vehicles, and road pavement shall be kept intentionally narrow at 17 to 20 feet to naturally reduce vehicle travel speeds. All intersections between local roads shall be constructed as three-way T-junctions, with no four-way cross intersections permitted.

numbers_en.k: Road segment that cannot be used as a shortcut by through traffic — for exclusive use by local residents
No single loop shall serve more than 50 vehicles
Pavement width — sufficiently narrow to naturally slow vehicle speeds

title: T JUNCTIONS
summary_en: Lay out the road system such that any two roads intersecting at-grade meet at three-way T JUNCTIONS as close to 90 degrees as possible. Four-way cross intersections and crossing through movements are avoided. This design follows geometric logic: when two two-way roads intersect at a full cross, there are 16 major conflict points, while a single T JUNCTIONS only has 3.

numbers_en.k: All at-grade intersections are built as three-way T JUNCTIONS as close to 90 degrees as possible
Four-way cross intersections have 16 conflict points, while T JUNCTIONS only have 3
No four-way cross intersections or crossing through movements are implemented

references: John Callender, Time-Saver Standards, Fourth Edition, New York, 1966, p. 1230.

title: GREEN STREETS
summary_en: On local streets that do not carry through traffic, the full length of the roadway is covered in grass, with only occasional paving stones embedded within the grass to provide a load-bearing surface for the wheels of vehicles that need to access the street. No demarcation is created between the street and adjacent sidewalk. Additional paving stones or gravel are laid at residential property entrances to allow vehicles to turn onto private residential lots. In typical low-density U.S. suburbs, more than 50% of the land area is covered by concrete or asphalt.

numbers_en.k: Entire local street surfaced with grass, with only two embedded paving strips for vehicle wheels to travel on
No distinction made between street and sidewalk
Over 50% of land in typical suburbs is covered by asphalt, and GREEN STREETS returns this share of land to grass

title: NETWORK OF PATHS AND CARS
summary_en: Unless traffic density is either extremely high or extremely low, arrange pedestrian paths at right angles to vehicular roads rather than parallel to them, so that pedestrian paths gradually form a second distinct NETWORK OF PATHS AND CARS orthogonal to the vehicular road system. This implementation can be carried out in a highly incremental manner, adding just one path at a time, as long as each path is placed mid-block to cross the vehicular roads. Conventional planning practices that fully separate pedestrians and vehicles end up causing adverse impacts to both user groups.

numbers_en.k: Pedestrian paths are arranged at right angles to vehicular roads to form two distinct independent networks
Pedestrian paths are sited through the center of blocks to cross vehicular roads, rather than running parallel along the roads
Instead of full segregation, the two networks are designed to meet at controlled intersection points

title: MAIN GATEWAYS
summary_en: In urban areas, every boundary of important humanistic significance — the edge of a building complex, a neighborhood, or a district — shall be marked by a grand MAIN GATEWAY at the point where the primary access route traverses this boundary. Many parts of towns and cities are surrounded by boundaries that usually exist in public perception, marking the end of one activity or place and the start of another.

numbers_en.k: Erect gateways at every intersection of a humanistically significant boundary and a primary access route
Arches, gate towers, paired columns, and symmetrically planted large trees can all serve as gateways

numbers_en.v: Crossing the threshold is an event
numbers_en.k: Gateways make the act of "entering a domain" a perceptible event

title: ROAD CROSSING
summary_en: Where a pedestrian path crosses a roadway with traffic volumes that impose more than 2 seconds of delay on crossing pedestrians, implement the ROAD CROSSING treatment. Narrow the roadway to only the width required for travel lanes, raise the sidewalk approximately 1 foot to extend continuously across the carriageway, and install a median refuge island between travel lanes. Grade the roadway upward toward the crossing point at a maximum 1:6 slope, and mark the crossing path with a canopy or shelter to make it clearly distinguishable.

numbers_en.v: Narrow to form the ROAD CROSSING node
numbers_en.k: Narrow the roadway at the crossing point to the width of only travel lanes
Raise the sidewalk by around 1 foot to run continuously across the roadway
Maximum gradient of the roadway rising toward the crossing point; refuge island and canopy to be installed

title: RAISED WALK
summary_en: Our conclusion is that any sidewalk arranged along a high-speed traffic road shall be a RAISED WALK approximately 18 inches above the road pavement, with its boundary demarcated by low walls, railings or balustrades. This RAISED WALK shall be placed on only one side of the road, and designed to be as wide as possible. This issue cannot be resolved by simply separating pedestrians and vehicles, as the inherent nature of pedestrians and vehicles means they will encounter each other at least occasionally.

numbers_en.k: Sidewalk along high-speed road is about 1.5 feet higher than the road surface
The edge of the RAISED WALK is demarcated with low walls, railings or balustrades

numbers_en.v: located on only one road side, as wide as possible
numbers_en.k: The RAISED WALK is set on only one side of the road and constructed to be as wide as possible

title: BIKE PATHS AND RACKS
summary_en: Establish a designated bike path network, where all bike paths are clearly marked with a distinct, easily identifiable pavement (such as red asphalt), and routed as far as possible along local streets or primary pedestrian paths. When bike paths run along local streets, their pavement may be flush with adjacent vehicle lanes, and placed on the sun-facing side where feasible; when they run along pedestrian paths, they shall be physically separated from pedestrian areas. Install bike racks at regular intervals along the full extent of the path network.

numbers_en.k: Bike paths are clearly marked with easily identifiable dedicated pavement (e.g. red asphalt)
Routes follow local streets or primary pedestrian paths as much as possible, on the sun-facing side
Bike racks are set at regular intervals along paths for parking

title: CHILDREN IN THE CITY
summary_en: As part of the bicycle lane network, a system of exceptionally safe routes is developed, fully segregated from motor vehicles, with traffic signals and pedestrian bridges at intersections, and lined with residences and shops that ensure constant natural surveillance of the route. These routes run through every neighborhood so children can access them without crossing major arterial roads, and extend across the entire city to pass through pedestrian streets, workshops, and assembly plants.

numbers_en.k: Child-specific routes are completely separated from motor vehicles, with intersections managed by traffic signals and pedestrian bridges

numbers_en.v: Many pairs of eyes watching the route
numbers_en.k: The route is lined with residences and shops, so there are always many pairs of eyes monitoring the road
Traverse the entire city and pass through every neighborhood, so children can access the routes without crossing major roads

title: CARNIVAL
summary_en: Reserve a portion of a town as a designated CARNIVAL zone, where raucous juggling, martial tournaments, performances, contests, dance, music, street theatre, clowns, drag acts, and public spectacles allow people to express their uninhibited, unruly sides. A wide pedestrian street runs through this zone, with stalls and narrow alleys arranged along its sides. An open-air theatre is sited at one end of the zone, and the theatre stage may be directly connected to the carnival street to enable the two spaces to interpenetrate and mutually nourish each other.

numbers_en.k: Reserve a portion of the town exclusively for CARNIVAL, a space for releasing uninhibited impulses

numbers_en.v: Wide pedestrian street traverses the zone
numbers_en.k: A wide pedestrian street runs through the CARNIVAL zone, flanked by stalls and narrow alleys
An open-air theatre is placed at one end of the zone, with its stage directly connected to the CARNIVAL street to support mutual interpenetration and reciprocal reinforcement

title: QUIET BACKS
summary_en: Provide buildings in busy town districts with a quiet QUIET BACKS zone at their rear, positioned far from noise sources. Construct a pedestrian path along this quiet rear, sited sufficiently far from adjacent buildings to receive ample sunlight, while noise is isolated by separating walls and setback distance. Ensure this path does not function as a natural shortcut for high-volume pedestrian flows, and connect it to other pedestrian routes to form a long continuous quiet alley corridor that links to local ponds and streams.

numbers_en.k: Allocate a noise-free quiet rear for buildings located in busy town sections

numbers_en.v: Adequate sunlight access and noise isolation
numbers_en.k: Rear pedestrian path is set far enough from buildings to obtain sufficient sunlight, with noise blocked by walls and setback distance
Ensure the path is not a natural shortcut for heavy pedestrian flows, and is connected to form a continuous quiet alley corridor

title: ACCESSIBLE GREEN
summary_en: Construct one open public ACCESSIBLE GREEN within a 3-minute (approximately 750-foot) walking distance of every residential unit and every workplace. This means these green spaces must be evenly spread across the entire city at roughly 1500-foot intervals, with each green space measuring at least 150 feet on each side and covering a minimum area of 60,000 square feet. Parks as commonly understood are excessively large and sparsely sited, so very few people live sufficiently close to them.

numbers_en.k: A green space is located within a 3-minute (approximately 750-foot) walking distance of every residential unit and every workplace
Green spaces are evenly distributed across the entire city at intervals of approximately 1500 feet
Each green space is no less than 150 feet on each side, with a minimum area of 60,000 square feet

title: SMALL PUBLIC SQUARES
summary_en: Design SMALL PUBLIC SQUARES far smaller than you initially envisage: their short dimension typically does not exceed 45 to 60 feet, and never exceeds 70 feet (this restriction applies exclusively to the short side width, while the long side can be longer). Every public street naturally expands at key nodes with the densest activity, and it is precisely these bulging, expanded small public squares that can accommodate genuine public life.

numbers_en.k: The width of the short side of the square, which typically does not exceed 45–60 feet
Absolute upper limit for the short side width (the long side can be longer)
Small public squares are the natural widening of streets at activity nodes, rather than independent oversized spaces

title: HIGH PLACES
summary_en: Occasional HIGH PLACES distributed across the city function as landmarks; these can be natural topographic elements, towers, or sections of the roof of the tallest local building, but all such sites must include a segment of physical climbing. Even the smallest village has a dominant landmark, typically a church tower, while large cities have hundreds of these landmarks. The instinct to build these towers is clearly not unique to Christianity, and the same practice has occurred repeatedly across different cultures.

numbers_en.k: Landmark HIGH PLACES scattered across the city, rather than a single large tower
Every HIGH PLACE must include a segment of physical climbing

numbers_en.v: Present even in the smallest villages
numbers_en.k: The smallest villages have a dominant landmark, while large cities have hundreds of such landmarks

title: DANCING IN THE STREET
summary_en: Along promenades, in plazas and night-time activity centers, build a slightly elevated platform as a bandstand for street musicians and local bands to perform, add a canopy to the platform, and potentially set up small refreshment stalls at ground level. Pave the area surrounding the bandstand with hard landscaping to create space for public dancing, with no admission fees charged. People across the world once danced in streets, and "DANCING IN THE STREET" is the imagery of supreme joy in theatre, songs and daily language.

numbers_en.k: A slightly elevated, covered platform for street musicians and local bands to perform

numbers_en.v: Hard paving laid around the perimeter
numbers_en.k: Hard paving installed around the bandstand for public dancing
Free of charge — this is public, spontaneous joy rather than a commercial performance

title: POOLS AND STREAMS
summary_en: Retain natural pools and streams and allow them to flow through the city, and construct waterfront pedestrian trails and pedestrian bridges across water to support public access to the water. Position streams as natural urban barriers, where motor vehicles only cross over on occasional bridges. Wherever possible, direct stormwater into open ditches to flow above ground along pedestrian trails and in front of building entrances, and install fountains in sites that have no natural running water.

numbers_en.k: Retain natural pools and streams and allow them to pass through the urban area
Build waterfront pedestrian paths and water-spanning pedestrian bridges for public water access
Collect rainwater into open ditches to flow above ground along pedestrian paths and in front of building entrances

title: BIRTH PLACES
summary_en: Establish local BIRTH PLACES for women to give birth. These sites are custom-tailored to frame childbirth as a natural, significant moment: entire families visit to receive prenatal care and education, while fathers and midwives provide companionship and support during labor. The core concept holds that "Pregnancy is not an emergency state, and mothers should not be expected to return to 'normal' right after childbirth ... it is a highly active, full-potential period of life."

numbers_en.k: Small BIRTH PLACES dispersed across communities, rather than centralized large hospitals
Whole families come to receive prenatal care and education, with fathers present during childbirth
Treat childbirth as a natural, joyful moment rather than an emergency requiring rescue

title: HOLY GROUND
summary_en: In every community and neighborhood, identify a specific HOLY GROUND site as sacred space, forming a series of nested courtyards where each tier is marked by a gateway, growing progressively more private and sacred moving inward, with the innermost space serving as the ultimate sanctuary that can only be reached by traversing all outer layers. Rituals tied to birth, coming of age, marriage, and death are critical to human growth, and these ceremonies cannot be properly held unless they are allocated appropriately suited dedicated sites.

numbers_en.k: A sequence of progressively inward courtyards connected by gateways
More private and more sacred moving inward, with the innermost space being the ultimate sanctuary
The innermost sanctuary can only be reached by passing through all outer gateways

title: COMMON LAND
summary_en: Designate 25% of the land within a residential cluster as COMMON LAND, placing it immediately adjacent to (or in extremely close proximity to) the dwellings that share it. The fundamental principle is to remain vigilant against motor vehicles: they must never be allowed to dominate this land. In pre-industrial societies, COMMON LAND between residences and workshops existed naturally, so it never required deliberate emphasis; the paths and streets leading to buildings were inherently safe, social spaces.

numbers_en.v: 25% of land is designated as COMMON LAND
numbers_en.k: One quarter of the land in the residential cluster is designated as COMMON LAND

numbers_en.v: Sited immediately adjacent to each household
numbers_en.k: The COMMON LAND is immediately adjacent to or extremely close to the dwellings that share it
Motor vehicles are never permitted to dominate this COMMON LAND

title: CONNECTED PLAY
summary_en: Arrange commons, pedestrian paths, gardens and small footbridges to connect at least 64 residential units via a no-through-traffic zone, and formalize this zone as the CONNECTED PLAY space for the children of these households. Children need the company of other children; a number of studies even indicate that their need for interaction with other children is greater than their need for their own mothers.

numbers_en.k: At least 64 households linked by one continuous corridor
This entire play zone does not intersect with vehicle lanes (crosses over via small footbridges)
Children's need for other children even exceeds their need for their mothers

title: PUBLIC OUTDOOR ROOM
summary_en: In every residential neighborhood and working community, convert a parcel of common land into a PUBLIC OUTDOOR ROOM: a partially enclosed space with partial roof coverage, supporting columns, no walls, and possibly a trellis. Locate this space adjacent to a key public path, within the view of a large number of surrounding homes and workshops. Adult residents seek out corner taverns to chat, drink and spend their leisure time, while adolescents, especially teenage boys, also select their own preferred street corners to loiter and wait for friends.

numbers_en.k: A partially enclosed PUBLIC OUTDOOR ROOM: features partial roof coverage, supporting columns, no walls
Placed next to a key public path, within the line of sight of many surrounding residences and workshops

numbers_en.v: may be fitted with a trellis
numbers_en.k: May be equipped with a vine-covered trellis

title: GRAVE SITES
summary_en: No large-scale cemeteries will be constructed. Instead, small parcels of land scattered across communities are designated as GRAVE SITES, sited at park corners, along road segments, in gardens, and beside building entrances, so that memorials for the deceased bearing inscriptions and commemorative artifacts can be placed respectfully to honor their lives. Each GRAVE SITE is assigned a clear boundary, an access path, and a quiet seating nook, and this land is consecrated per customary practice. The massive sprawling cemeteries on the urban outskirts have expelled death from everyday life.

numbers_en.v: No large cemeteries will be built
numbers_en.k: Do not concentrate the deceased in giant suburban cemeteries

numbers_en.v: Distributed across all parts of the community
numbers_en.k: Allocate small individual grave plots to park corners, road segments, gardens, and beside building entrances
Provide each grave site with a boundary, a small path, and a quiet corner for sitting

title: STILL WATER
summary_en: Provide one STILL WATER feature — a pond or a pool — for swimming in every neighborhood. Keep the pool permanently open to the public, with access restricted exclusively to the shallow end, so that water depth increases gradually starting from just one or two inches. As explained in *Ponds and Streams* (64), direct contact with water is critically important, and ordinary local water bodies, when properly managed, can become one of the area's most valuable resources.

numbers_en.k: Each neighborhood is provided with one swimmable STILL WATER feature

numbers_en.v: Access via the shallow end only
numbers_en.k: Entrances are restricted to the shallow end, and the pool depth increases gradually starting from 1 to 2 inches
The pool remains open and free of charge to the public at all times

title: LOCAL SPORTS
summary_en: Disperse venues for team and individual sports across every workplace community and residential neighborhood, including facilities for tennis, squash, table tennis, swimming, billiards, basketball, dance, and fitness training, and make these sports spaces visible to passersby as an open invitation to participate. In agricultural societies, people used their bodies in many different ways in daily life. In urban societies, however, the majority of people only exercise their minds rather than their bodies, or use their bodies in only a handful of limited ways.

numbers_en.k: All types of sports venues are distributed across every community and neighborhood, rather than being concentrated in a single large stadium
Make sports activities visible to passersby as an invitation for participation
Multiple venue types supporting tennis, squash, table tennis, swimming, billiards, basketball, dance, gym and other activities

title: ADVENTURE PLAYGROUND
summary_en: One ADVENTURE PLAYGROUND is designated for children in each neighborhood: it is not a refined playground with asphalt paving and swings, but a site furnished with various raw materials including nets, boxes, buckets, trees, ropes, simple tools, frames, grass and water, enabling children to create and recreate their own play spaces. Play serves multiple functions: it gives children opportunities to gather together, move their bodies, exercise their muscles, and test new skills.

numbers_en.v: Raw materials instead of finished products
numbers_en.k: Provide raw materials including nets, boxes, buckets, trees, ropes, tools, frames, grass, water, etc.
Allow children to create and recreate their own playground
Set up one such ADVENTURE PLAYGROUND for children in every neighborhood

title: ANIMALS
summary_en: Legislation permits people to keep any animal on their private plot or in their private stable; a fenced, protected commons is established to let animals graze freely, with grass, trees and water provided on site, and at least one fully asphalt-free circulation system is constructed in the neighborhood, where animal dung can fall naturally without the need for cleaning. While there is widespread recognition that communities need "parks", the more essential underlying demand is for residents to have regular daily contact with animals.

numbers_en.k: Legislation permits residents to keep any animal on their private plot or in private stables
Designate a fenced, protected commons with grass, trees and water for free animal grazing
At least one fully asphalt-free circulation system that allows animal dung to fall naturally without cleaning

title: THE FAMILY
summary_en: Establish a set of processes to encourage groups of 8 to 12 people to gather and form co-living households under THE FAMILY pattern. Three core morphological elements are critical: (1) Private domains for the small groups and individuals that constitute this extended household, including the couple’s domain, private rooms, and sub-units for nuclear families; (2) Public spaces for shared functions, including cooking, working, gardening, and childcare; (3) A shared gathering space located at a key intersection on the site.

numbers_en.k: Encourage 8 to 12 people to gather to form co-living households
Private domains for individual small groups and persons (couple’s domain, private rooms, nuclear family sub-units)
Public spaces for shared functions (cooking / working / gardening / childcare) + public gathering space at key site intersections

title: HOUSE FOR A SMALL FAMILY
summary_en: Divide the house into three distinct parts: a domain for parents, a domain for children, and a public zone. The three domains are conceived to be roughly similar in size, with the public zone being the largest. Many small families that are not large enough to accommodate a formal nursery and not affluent enough to hire a nanny find their daily lives overwhelmed by their children, as children naturally want to stay close to adults while parents lack the extra energy to separate their own spaces from their children's.

numbers_en.k: Parent domain + Child domain + Public zone
The three domains are similar in size, with the public zone being the largest
Parents and children each have their own exclusive domain, and share the central public zone

title: HOUSE FOR A COUPLE
summary_en: Conceptualize HOUSE FOR A COUPLE as a program consisting of two categories of spaces: a shared couple domain, and separate independent private worlds for each partner. The shared domain is defined as semi-public and semi-private, while each private world is fully individual and completely private. Couples naturally need a shared domain where they can conduct joint activities, host friends, and spend intimate time together, but each person also requires a private world that belongs entirely to themselves.

numbers_en.k: Semi-public and semi-private: for joint cooking, receiving guests, and intimate couple time
One fully individual, completely private space per person
HOUSE FOR A COUPLE is composed of the two combined categories of shared and private spaces

title: HOUSE FOR ONE PERSON
summary_en: Conceive the HOUSE FOR ONE PERSON as an extremely simple space, essentially a single-room cottage or studio surrounded by alcoves of varying sizes. At its most compact, the entire dwelling may be no more than 300 to 400 square feet. The housing market offers almost no purpose-built houses or apartments designed exclusively for one person; people who choose to live alone often occupy larger units originally constructed for two to three occupants.

numbers_en.k: essentially a single-room cottage or studio

numbers_en.v: surrounded by alcoves on all sides
numbers_en.k: The main space is surrounded by alcoves of varying sizes (sleeping/reading/cooking/window seat)
At its most compact, the entire dwelling is no more than 300 to 400 square feet

title: YOUR OWN HOME
summary_en: Make every possible effort to render traditional rental forms unfeasible and even illegal, so that every household is provided with their own home with sufficient land to construct a garden. The definition of ownership under the YOUR OWN HOME framework places core emphasis on "control rights" rather than financial ownership. All locations that can establish such an ownership structure that enables residents to control their own houses and gardens while eliminating financial speculation shall prioritize these ownership forms.

numbers_en.k: Guarantee every household a self-owned home with sufficient land to build a garden
Ownership prioritizes control rights rather than financial ownership and speculation
Residents can personally renovate, plant, and maintain their own unique home

title: SELF-GOVERNING WORKSHOPS AND OFFICES
summary_en: Encourage the formation of SELF-GOVERNING WORKSHOPS AND OFFICES staffed by 5 to 20 workers each. Each group retains full autonomy over its organization, operational style, relationships with other groups, hiring and dismissal decisions, and work schedules. When work is complex and requires a larger organizational setup, several such work groups may combine and collaborate to jointly produce complex products and services. A person will only enjoy their work when they understand the full context of the whole process and maintain direct control over their own work.

numbers_en.k: 5 to 20 workers per self-governing workshop/office
Full group autonomy over organization, style, hiring and firing, and work schedules
Multiple work groups may combine and collaborate when work is complex

title: SMALL SERVICES WITHOUT RED TAPE
summary_en: In any institution that delivers public services via its constituent departments, implement the four tenets of SMALL SERVICES WITHOUT RED TAPE: (1) Make each service or department as autonomous as possible; (2) Cap the total number of staff for any single service at no more than 12 people; (3) Assign each service a clearly identifiable section within the building; (4) Locate each service directly adjacent to a public access route. A substantial body of existing literature documents how red tape and bureaucratic structures run counter to human needs.

numbers_en.k: Each service/department is as autonomous as possible
Total number of staff for any single service does not exceed 12 people
Each occupies a distinct identifiable space and directly abuts a public access route

references: Gideon Sjoberg, Richard Brymer, and Buford Farris, “Bureaucracy and the Lower Class.”

title: OFFICE CONNECTIONS
summary_en: To determine the distance between different departments, first calculate the number of daily round trips between every pair of departments, then look up the "trouble distance" from the relevant chart, and ensure the physical distance between the two departments is less than this trouble distance. One flight of stairs is counted as approximately 100 feet, and two flights of stairs as approximately 300 feet. Current architectural planning practice commonly uses a proximity matrix to address this problem.

numbers_en.v: Determine distance by round trip frequency
numbers_en.k: The more frequent the daily round trips between two departments, the shorter their physical distance should be
The physical distance must be smaller than the "trouble distance" derived from the number of round trips
One flight of stairs is approximately equivalent to 100 feet, and two flights of stairs approximately 300 feet

title: MASTER AND APPRENTICES
summary_en: Arrange work in every working group, industry and office such that work and learning progress side by side, treating every individual task as a learning opportunity. To this end, organize work around the MASTER AND APPRENTICES tradition, and support this form of social organization through spatial partitioning: divide workspaces into discrete spatial clusters, each occupied by one master and his apprentices, where the group can work and communicate together. This is the simplest method for knowledge acquisition.

numbers_en.k: Enable work and learning to advance side by side, with every task serving as a learning opportunity
Organize work around the MASTER AND APPRENTICES tradition

numbers_en.v: One Cluster for One Master-Apprentice Unit
numbers_en.k: Workspaces are divided into spatial clusters, with one master and his apprentices assigned to each cluster

title: TEENAGE SOCIETY
summary_en: Replace the traditional high school with an institution that is essentially a model of adult society, where students take on most responsibilities for their learning and social life, with clearly defined roles and disciplinary frameworks. Adults provide guidance for learning and the structural operation of this TEENAGE SOCIETY, but as much operational control as possible is retained in the hands of the students themselves. The most distinct traditional example of this model documented to date comes from a self-governing adolescent community.

numbers_en.k: Replace traditional high schools with an institution that acts as a miniature model of adult society
Students take on most responsibilities for learning and social life, with clearly defined roles
Adults provide guidance, while keeping decision-making authority in students' hands to the maximum possible extent

title: SHOPFRONT SCHOOLS
summary_en: Do not construct large public schools for children aged 7 to 12; instead, establish small independent schools one after another. Keep schools at a very small scale to cut operating costs and maintain a 1:1 student-teacher ratio. Locate these schools in the public section of the community, occupying one street-facing shopfront plus three to four rooms. The most suitable environment for children is the community itself, just as the most ideal environment for an infant to learn to speak is their own home.

numbers_en.v: A series of small independent schools
numbers_en.k: No large public schools are built; small independent schools are established one after another
Small school size ensures low operating costs and supports a stable 1:1 student-teacher ratio
Sited in the public portion of the community, consisting of one street-facing shopfront plus three to four rooms

title: CHILDREN'S HOME
summary_en: Never construct large, institutional CHILDREN'S HOME facilities. It is undoubtedly best for children to stay in their own family homes, but when children do require alternative residential placement, build small, home-like spaces for them that are deeply embedded in the local community, where a small group of children is cared for by one consistent, permanent caregiver.
