Keep these facilities small, so they operate more like an extended family rather than a formal institution.

numbers_en.k: Never build large institutional CHILDREN'S HOMEs, only develop small, home-like residential accommodations
A small group of children is cared for by one permanent, on-site resident caregiver
Deeply integrated into the local community, functioning more like an extended family than an institution

references: Anna Freud and Dorothy Burlingham, Infants Without Families.

title: INDIVIDUALLY OWNED SHOPS
summary_en: Do everything possible to encourage the growth of small INDIVIDUALLY OWNED SHOPS, and discourage large chain stores. Only when a local area has a large number of competing stores that are each small in size can these businesses truly serve people's needs. The more chain stores there are and the larger each individual store is, the worse the service people can obtain will be.

numbers_en.k: Make every effort to encourage small individually owned shops and discourage large chain stores
A large number of competing stores that are each small in size can truly serve people's needs

numbers_en.v: More chain stores lead to worse service
numbers_en.k: The more chain stores there are and the larger each individual store is, the worse the service people receive will be

title: STREET CAFE
summary_en: Encourage the establishment of local STREET CAFE venues within residential communities. Each such cafe shall be developed into a distinct, exclusive space for its regular patrons. Seating layouts are configured to allow groups of visitors to stay for a full day while watching the world go by, with street-facing seats opening directly onto the sidewalk to facilitate mutual connection between seated patrons and passing pedestrians.

numbers_en.k: Each STREET CAFE serves as a dedicated space belonging to its regular customers

numbers_en.v: Sit and watch the world go by
numbers_en.k: Seating arrangements allow people to stay for a full day and observe the surrounding street scene
Sidewalk-facing seats open directly to the pedestrian walkway to enable connection between seated patrons and passersby

title: CORNER GROCERY
summary_en: Site one CORNER GROCERY for every residential cluster, positioned along a major active street, and located no more than a few hundred yards from the majority of households. Do not place the grocery at destinations that residents are already obligated to travel to; instead, site it at locations that people naturally pass by and can enter as a casual, convenient stop. Wherever feasible, arrange for the storekeeper to live in the unit directly above the shop or immediately adjacent to the store premises.

numbers_en.k: One small grocery store allocated per residential cluster, located no more than a few hundred yards from most households
Positioned along major active streets, sited at locations that people naturally pass by
Arrange for the storekeeper to live on the floor above the shop or immediately adjacent to the store wherever possible

title: BEER HALL
summary_en: Site public drinking establishments across all areas of the town, including beer halls, bars, and taverns, where people can gather to drink and enjoy casual, lively social interaction. Do not design these venues to be overly neat or overly compartmentalized; arrange seating as large communal long tables that allow strangers to sit side by side and become temporary drinking companions. Host multiple concurrent activities including music, dance, chess, and darts within the same shared space.

numbers_en.k: Distribute beer halls and bars across the town to allow people to gather for casual lively socializing

numbers_en.v: Communal seating at large long tables
numbers_en.k: Arrange seating as large long tables so that strangers can sit side by side and become temporary drinking companions
Run multiple activities including music, dance, chess and darts concurrently in the same space

title: TRAVELLER'S INN
summary_en: Operate the TRAVELLER'S INN as an overnight accommodation space for travellers, which distinguishes itself from most hotels and motels in that all its vitality stems from the small community composed of travellers who happen to lodge there on that exact night. The inn is kept at a small scale, accommodating 30 to 40 guests per property; meals are served in shared dining arrangements, and a common living room and courtyard are provided for travellers who meet by chance to get acquainted with each other.

numbers_en.k: Small-scale, each inn only accommodates 30 to 40 guests
Meals are served in shared dining arrangements, with a common living room and courtyard provided
The inn's vitality comes from the small community formed by travellers staying there on the same night

title: BUS STOP
summary_en: Build each BUS STOP into a small public life center, making them part of the gateways leading to neighborhoods, work communities, and all sections of the town. Select optimal locations to allow the BUS STOP to operate in conjunction with several other types of adjacent activities: it shall be equipped with at least one newsstand, area map, outdoor shelter, and seating, and remain connected to surrounding activities under all circumstances.

numbers_en.k: Build BUS STOPs into small public life centers and neighborhood gateways
Equipped with at least a newsstand, map, outdoor shelter and seating
Site the BUS STOP to function synergistically with other adjacent activities

title: FOOD STANDS
summary_en: Concentrate FOOD STANDS at the intersections of vehicular carriageways and pedestrian walkways. These facilities may take the form of movable vending carts, small sheds, or units embedded in the street-facing facade of buildings that are partially open to the street. This arrangement allows people to purchase food conveniently nearby and eat while standing.

numbers_en.k: Concentrate FOOD STANDS at the intersections of carriageways and pedestrian walkways

numbers_en.v: Vending cart / small shed / facade-embedded unit
numbers_en.k: Movable vending carts, small sheds, or units embedded in street-facing building facades
Partially open to the street, enabling nearby food purchase and standing consumption

title: SLEEPING IN PUBLIC
summary_en: Ensure public environments are consistently stocked with an ample supply of benches, comfortable resting destinations, nooks suitable for squatting, and sand areas that support comfortable full-body reclining. These spaces should be designed to be relatively secluded, separated from vehicular traffic, possibly elevated one step above the surrounding ground level, and fitted with seating and grass patches to allow visitors to slouch comfortably, read newspapers, and take short naps.

numbers_en.k: Public environments are fully furnished with sufficient benches and nooks that support both sitting and lying
Designed to be relatively secluded, separated from vehicular traffic, and possibly elevated one single step
Equipped with seating and grassy areas to allow users to slouch, read newspapers, and take naps

title: BUILDING COMPLEX
summary_en: Never construct oversized monolithic single buildings. Whenever feasible, translate your architectural program into a BUILDING COMPLEX, so that all its individual parts manifest the genuine social realities of the specific context. In low-density areas, the complex appears as a cluster of separate small buildings linked by access paths, connecting corridors and courtyards, each corresponding to a distinct real internal social unit.

numbers_en.k: Prohibition on constructing oversized single monolithic buildings
Translate the architectural program into a BUILDING COMPLEX
Each component corresponds to a real internal social unit, connected via connecting corridors and courtyards

title: NUMBER OF STORIES
summary_en: First calculate the total gross floor area in square feet you require, then divide that value by the site area to obtain the Floor Area Ratio (FAR). Next, select your building height from the reference comparison table based on the calculated FAR and the heights of surrounding buildings. Under no circumstances shall the ground footprint covered by the building exceed 50% of the total lot area. Per empirical guidance, the maximum FAR for 1 NUMBER OF STORIES is approximately 0.5, 2 NUMBER OF STORIES roughly 1.0, 3 NUMBER OF STORIES around 1.5, and 4 NUMBER OF STORIES roughly 2.0.

numbers_en.k: Under no circumstances may the building's ground footprint exceed 50% of the lot area
Set building NUMBER OF STORIES based on FAR and surrounding building heights, rather than pursuing maximum height blindly
1 NUMBER OF STORIES ≈ 0.5, 2 NUMBER OF STORIES ≈ 1.0, 3 NUMBER OF STORIES ≈ 1.5, 4 NUMBER OF STORIES ≈ 2.0

references: Christopher Alexander, “The Effect of High Buildings.”

title: SHIELDED PARKING
summary_en: All large surface parking lots and parking structures are situated behind a type of natural screening wall, so that vehicles and parking facilities are fully obscured from external public view. The screening wall enclosing the parking area may be a standalone building, row houses, grass-covered earthen mounds or berms, or commercial storefronts. The parking lot entrance is designed as a natural access gateway to the building it serves, and positioned in a highly visible location.

numbers_en.k: Large surface parking lots/parking structures placed behind walls, vehicles not visible from outside

numbers_en.v: Screening walls are houses, berms and stores
numbers_en.k: Enclosure walls may be buildings, row houses, grass-covered earthen mounds, or storefronts
Parking entrance designed as natural gateway to the served building, placed in easily visible location

title: CIRCULATION REALMS
summary_en: When laying out large buildings or building complexes, people traveling to a specific interior point will sequentially pass through a continuous series of CIRCULATION REALMS. Each of these realms is demarcated by a gateway, and each subsequent realm is smaller than the prior one as users move through the gateway of one realm to enter the next. These realms are selected to be easily named, so that a person can be guided to the destination simply by telling them which specific realm to go to.

numbers_en.k: Sequentially pass through a series of realms to reach the interior
Each realm is marked by a gateway, with each subsequent realm smaller than the previous one
Each realm can be easily named to facilitate wayfinding

title: MAIN BUILDING
summary_en: For any group of buildings, first identify which structure houses the most essential functions, namely which one acts as the soul of the building cluster as a human institution. Then design this structure as the MAIN BUILDING, placing it at the central position and equipping it with a taller roof. Even if the building cluster is so densely integrated that it forms a single whole building, its primary section shall be constructed taller and more prominent than the rest, so that its core status can be recognized at a glance.

numbers_en.k: Determine which building houses the most essential functions and serves as the soul of this building cluster

numbers_en.v: Centrally located with a taller roof
numbers_en.k: Shape it into the MAIN BUILDING: set it at the central position with a taller roof
Even if the cluster is integrated into a single building, make its main section taller and more prominent

title: PEDESTRIAN STREET
summary_en: Arrange buildings to enclose a PEDESTRIAN STREET, which is fitted with numerous entrances and open staircases that run directly from upper floors down to street level. This configuration ensures that even movement between individual rooms takes place outdoors, rather than being restricted to movement only between separate buildings. At present, a large share of pedestrian movement is confined to indoor corridors and lobbies instead of occurring outdoors, a phenomenon driven both by the takeover of streets by motor vehicles, and by indoor corridors that reinforce this same retreat from outdoor public space.

numbers_en.k: arrange buildings to enclose a PEDESTRIAN STREET with multiple entrances along the street
open staircases leading directly from upper floors to street level
even movement between rooms takes place outdoors in a car-free environment

title: BUILDING THOROUGHFARE
summary_en: Whenever density or climatic conditions force primary circulation routes to be situated indoors, construct them as BUILDING THOROUGHFARE. Locate each thoroughfare in a position that serves as a shortcut, ensure it maintains maximum possible continuity with external public streets, and provide it with spacious, open entrances. Line both sides of the thoroughfare with windows, seating, counters, and entrances protruding into the adjacent hall, so that interior life opens onto the passage, making it operate as a genuine public street rather than a lifeless corridor.

numbers_en.v: Indoor circulation routes converted into interior streets
numbers_en.k: Develop routes as BUILDING THOROUGHFARE when density or climate requires circulation to be placed indoors
Position to function as a shortcut, maintain continuity with external public streets, set spacious open entrances

numbers_en.v: Windows, seating, counters and entrances along both edges
numbers_en.k: Line both sides with windows, seats, counters and outward-protruding entrances

title: FAMILY OF ENTRANCES
summary_en: Arrange a group of closely positioned entrances to form a FAMILY OF ENTRANCES. This arrangement meets two core criteria: (1) the entrances form a unified cluster that can be perceived as a single collective, and every individual entrance is visible from all other entrances in the group; (2) all entrances are largely similar in form, for instance all are porches, all are doors embedded in a wall, or all are marked by entryways of a consistent, matching style. This allows arriving visitors to immediately identify that this set of entrances belong to one another as a cohesive group.

numbers_en.k: Closely spaced entrances form a single group that can be viewed as a whole
Each entrance is visible from every other entrance in the group
All are porches / all are wall-mounted doors / all feature matching entryways, with consistent overall design

title: SMALL PARKING LOTS
summary_en: Design each SMALL PARKING LOT to hold no more than 5 to 7 vehicles, and enclose every lot with low garden walls, hedges, fences, gentle slopes and trees so that parked vehicles are almost entirely hidden from view from the outside. Space these small parking lots a minimum of 100 feet apart from one another.

numbers_en.k: Each parking lot accommodates no more than 5 to 7 vehicles

numbers_en.v: Screened by low garden walls and hedges
numbers_en.k: Enclosed by garden walls, hedges, fences, gentle slopes and trees, parked vehicles are nearly invisible from outside
These small parking lots are spaced at least 100 feet apart from each other

title: SITE REPAIR
summary_en: Treat the site and all buildings situated on it as a single, living ecosystem. Retain the most valuable, healthiest, and finest parts of the site completely untouched, and locate buildings on the currently most uninviting, barren and degraded portions of the site. This construction practice implements SITE REPAIR, making the entire site healthier and more integrated, rather than damaging its best existing sections.

numbers_en.k: Treat the site and its buildings as a single, living ecosystem
Keep the most valuable, healthy and high-quality site sections completely unaltered
Locate buildings on the most uninhabitable, barren and damaged sections of the site

title: SOUTH FACING OUTDOORS
summary_en: Always site a building to the north of its corresponding adjacent outdoor space, so that the outdoor space occupies the south-facing, sunlit side of the building. Never create a long, continuous deep shadow zone between the building and the sun-exposed portion of the outdoor area. This is arguably the single most important principle for building layout: if a building is positioned correctly, people will use the adjacent outdoor space, while if sited incorrectly, that outdoor area will in most cases be functionally inactive and unused.

numbers_en.v: Building positioned on the north side
numbers_en.k: Always place the building on the north side of its associated outdoor space

numbers_en.v: Outdoor space on the south side for full solar access
numbers_en.k: Reserve the south side for the outdoor space to receive full sun exposure

numbers_en.v: No long deep shadow strip retained
numbers_en.k: Never leave a long deep shadow strip between the building and the sun-facing outdoor area

title: POSITIVE OUTDOOR SPACE
summary_en: Make every outdoor space situated between and surrounding your buildings a POSITIVE OUTDOOR SPACE. Introduce a certain degree of enclosure to each space, wrapping every space with building wings, trees, hedges, fences, arcades, and pergola walkways. Continue this treatment until the space becomes a distinct entity with positive qualities, rather than spilling out infinitely along building corners.

numbers_en.k: Make all outdoor spaces between and around buildings positive
Enclose each space with building wings, trees, hedges, fences, arcades, and pergolas

numbers_en.v: Convex form with no unconstrained spillage
numbers_en.k: Until it becomes an entity with a convex boundary and no longer spills out infinitely along building corners

title: WINGS OF LIGHT
summary_en: Arrange every individual building to be divided into several wings, with each wing roughly corresponding to the most important natural social groups inside the building. Design each wing to be as long and narrow as possible, with a width that never exceeds 25 feet. A massive monolithic building that disregards interior daylight traps people in deep internal darkness, while the long and narrow WINGS OF LIGHT allow natural daylight to reach every part of the interior.

numbers_en.k: Divide each building into multiple wings corresponding to internal natural social groups
Each wing is designed to be as long and narrow as possible
Width never exceeds 25 feet to ensure daylight reaches all interior spaces

title: CONNECTED BUILDINGS
summary_en: Wherever feasible, connect new buildings to the surrounding existing built structures. Do not leave setback gaps between adjacent buildings; instead, design new construction as a direct continuation of older existing buildings. Even in medium- and high-density areas where buildings are sited in close proximity and there is sufficient rationale for forming a unified contiguous built mass, practitioners still stubbornly build isolated structures surrounded by unutilized, functionally useless open space.

numbers_en.k: Connect new buildings to surrounding existing buildings wherever possible
Do not retain setback gaps between buildings

numbers_en.v: Extended to form a contiguous whole
numbers_en.k: Design new buildings as a continuation of older buildings to form a continuous built fabric

title: LONG THIN HOUSE
summary_en: For small buildings, do not cluster all rooms into a single compact mass; instead, arrange rooms sequentially one after another, to maximize the distance between every two adjacent rooms as much as possible. This arrangement can be implemented horizontally, producing a LONG THIN HOUSE floor plan that is a long, narrow rectangle, or implemented vertically, producing a tall, narrow tower form. In either case, the building can be exceptionally narrow while remaining fully usable, with widths of 8 feet, 10 feet, and 12 feet all completely viable.

numbers_en.v: Rooms are arranged sequentially instead of being clustered
numbers_en.k: Do not cluster all rooms in a small house, arrange them one after another in sequence

numbers_en.v: Long thin rectangle / tall narrow tower
numbers_en.k: The floor plan forms a long thin rectangle, or the building forms a tall narrow tower
The building can be surprisingly narrow while still being functional, 8 ft, 10 ft and 12 ft widths are all viable

title: MAIN ENTRANCE
summary_en: Place the building's MAIN ENTRANCE at a location that is immediately visible from the primary approach, and give it a bold, prominent form that projects out in front of the building. The position of the MAIN ENTRANCE governs the layout of the entire building: it controls the circulation of people entering and exiting the structure, and all other layout-related decisions are derived from this positioning. When the entrance is sited correctly, the full layout unfolds naturally and simply; if sited incorrectly, every subsequent arrangement will feel awkward and misaligned.

numbers_en.k: Locate MAIN ENTRANCE at position immediately visible from primary approach
Assign MAIN ENTRANCE a bold, prominent form projecting forward of the building
MAIN ENTRANCE position governs the entire building's layout and circulation

title: HALF-HIDDEN GARDEN
summary_en: Do not place the garden entirely in front of the house, nor entirely behind it. Instead, situate it in an intermediate position alongside the house, as a HALF-HIDDEN GARDEN that is partially screened from the street, delivering both privacy and unobstructed access to natural daylight. Fully street-facing front gardens typically serve only ornamental purposes and are rarely used for occupancy, while fully enclosed back gardens are disconnected from daily living activities, making the semi-concealed side yard the only garden space that receives actual regular use.

numbers_en.v: neither fully front nor fully rear
numbers_en.k: the garden is placed neither entirely in front of the house nor entirely behind the house
arranged in an intermediate position adjacent to and parallel with the house
partially screened from the street, with both privacy and access to natural daylight

title: ENTRANCE TRANSITION
summary_en: Create an ENTRANCE TRANSITION space between the street and the building’s front door. Route the path connecting the street to the building entrance through this transition space, and demarcate it with a series of variations: shifts in light, sound, direction, footway paving, elevation, potentially gateways that modify the sense of enclosure, and most importantly, changes in visual field. The experience of entering a building directly influences how occupants perceive the interior space once they are inside.

numbers_en.k: Create an ENTRANCE TRANSITION space between the street and the front door

numbers_en.v: Route the path through the space
numbers_en.k: Guide the path connecting the street and the entrance through this ENTRANCE TRANSITION space
Demarcate the space with changes in light, sound, direction, paving, elevation, gateway-formed enclosure, and most notably, view

title: CAR CONNECTION
summary_en: Arrange the parking space and main entrance in a configuration where the shortest path from a parked car into the house, whether heading to the kitchen or the living room, always passes through the main entrance. Design the parking space as a genuine "room": a positive, elegant space purpose-built for vehicle parking, rather than merely a bare opening cut into the ground. Since people will always use the door closest to their parked car, the entrance nearest the parking area will eventually become the de facto main entrance.

numbers_en.v: Shortest path passes through main entrance
numbers_en.k: The shortest route from the car to the kitchen and living room always passes through the main entrance
Design the parking space as a genuine room, a positive and elegant place
Rather than just an opening cut into the ground surface

references: Vere Hole, et al., “Studies of 800 Houses in Conventional and Radburn Layouts.”

title: HIERARCHY OF OPEN SPACE
summary_en: Regardless of the type of space you are shaping — garden, terrace, street, park, public outdoor room or courtyard — ensure two conditions are met. (1) Construct at least one smaller space that looks into the target space and forms a natural "back" for it. (2) Arrange the space and its openings so that it looks out onto at least one larger space. This forms the core logic of the HIERARCHY OF OPEN SPACE, where every outdoor space is equipped with a natural "back".

numbers_en.v: smaller space acting as the back
numbers_en.k: construct at least one smaller space that looks into the target space and forms a natural back for it
arrange the space and its openings so that it looks out onto at least one larger space
as a result, every outdoor space has both a back and an orientation toward a larger space

title: COURTYARDS WHICH LIVE
summary_en: Arrange each courtyard so that it commands a view out to a larger open space, with at least two or three doors leading from the surrounding building into it, and the natural pedestrian paths connecting these doors traverse the courtyard. A covered loggia or porch shall be constructed on one side of the courtyard, immediately adjacent to one of the doors, to form a seamless connection with both the indoor space and the courtyard. Dead courtyards that are fully enclosed on four sides, have no through paths, and offer no outward views will be left unused by occupants.

numbers_en.v: View out to a larger open space
numbers_en.k: Design the courtyard to have an outward view to a certain larger open space

numbers_en.v: At least two or three doors lead to the courtyard
numbers_en.k: At least two or three doors lead from the building to the courtyard, with natural paths traversing the courtyard

numbers_en.v: Covered loggia/porch set on one side
numbers_en.k: Build a covered loggia or porch adjacent to a door on one side, integrating with both the indoor space and the courtyard

title: CASCADE OF ROOFS
summary_en: Envision the entire standalone building or building complex as a unified roof system. Place the largest, highest, and widest roof over the most important part of the building. When refining the roof layout, all smaller roofs can cascade down in successive tiers from these large primary roofs, forming a stable, self-supporting CASCADE OF ROOFS system that corresponds to the hierarchy of social spaces beneath it.

numbers_en.v: Entire building constitutes a roof system
numbers_en.k: Envision the entire individual building or building complex as a single roof system

numbers_en.v: Large roof covers the most significant area
numbers_en.k: Place the largest, highest, and widest roof over the most important portion of the building

numbers_en.v: Small roofs cascade down in successive tiers
numbers_en.k: Smaller roofs cascade down from large roofs in successive tiers, form a self-supporting system, and align with the social space hierarchy

title: SHELTERING ROOF
summary_en: Construct the roof as a pitched or vaulted form with its entire surface fully visible, and set the eaves to a very low height — at entrances and other spots where people stop and linger, the eave height drops as low as 6 ft or 6 ft 6 in. The top floor of each wing is built directly into the roof structure, so that the SHELTERING ROOF does not merely sit atop the space below, but fully embraces, encloses and covers that top level. A pitched roof or large overroof that is only added on top of an existing structure cannot generate this specific sense of shelter.

numbers_en.v: Pitched roof / vaulted roof, fully exposed roof surface
numbers_en.k: Form the roof as a pitched or vaulted roof, make the entire roof surface fully visible
Set the eaves to a very low height, with eave heights at entrances as low as approximately 6 feet

numbers_en.v: Top floor integrated into the roof
numbers_en.k: Build the top floor directly into the roof, so that the roof embraces it rather than merely covering it

title: ROOF GARDEN
summary_en: Reserve a usable portion of nearly every roof system as a ROOF GARDEN. Level these designated sections, or shape them into terraces for planting, and provide private spaces that accommodate both sitting and lying. Arrange ROOF GARDENS at varying floor heights, and guarantee that users can walk out directly to the ROOF GARDEN from the inhabited parts of the building at all times.

numbers_en.v: Reserve garden space on nearly every roof
numbers_en.k: Allocate a portion of almost every roof system for ROOF GARDEN use

numbers_en.v: Leveled, terraced, sitting and lying permitted
numbers_en.k: Level the designated areas, form terraces for planting, and set up private spaces for sitting and lying

numbers_en.v: Distributed across different floors, direct exterior access available
numbers_en.k: Place ROOF GARDENS at different floor levels, ensure direct access from the building's occupied residential areas

title: ARCADES
summary_en: Wherever a path runs along the edge of a building, arcades are constructed. First and foremost, these arcades connect buildings to one another, so that people can move from one location to another fully under the shelter of the arcades. Arcades are a semi-open transitional zone between the building and the external public realm: they extend interior life outward, while genuinely inviting the public to approach.

numbers_en.k: Construct arcades at all locations where paths run along building edges
Prioritize using arcades to connect separate buildings to one another

numbers_en.v: Move between locations under covered shelter
numbers_en.k: Enable people to walk from one place to another under the shelter of arcades

title: PATHS AND GOALS
summary_en: To arrange the PATHS AND GOALS layout, first place "goals" at each natural point of interest. Then connect these goals to one another to form paths, which may be straight or gently curved between goals, with their paving flaring out around each goal. The distance between any two goals must never exceed several hundred feet.

numbers_en.k: Place goals at all natural points of interest first
Connect goals to one another to form paths, which may be straight or gently curved
Paving flares out around goals, and the spacing between goals does not exceed several hundred feet

title: PATH SHAPE
summary_en: Bulge the mid-section of a public path and narrow its two ends, so that the path itself forms an enclosed area: a place for lingering, rather than merely a thoroughfare for passing through. For centuries, streets have provided usable public space for urban dwellers right outside the doors of their residences. Today, however, modern cities have, through a range of subtle approaches, turned streets into spaces that exist "for passing through" rather than "for lingering".

numbers_en.k: Create a bulging shape at the mid-section of the public path
Make the two ends of the path relatively narrow
Make the path itself enclose a stayable space instead of functioning solely as a thoroughfare for passing through

title: BUILDING FRONTS
summary_en: No setbacks are permitted between any street, path, or public open space and the buildings constructed adjacent to it. Setback open areas have no value, and almost always undermine the value of the open zone between adjacent buildings. Construct buildings all the way to the edge of the path; for communities where outdated regulations prevent this implementation, revise the relevant laws. In addition, arrange BUILDING FRONTS to follow the shape of the street, presenting slightly irregular staggered angles.

numbers_en.k: No setbacks are reserved between streets/paths/open spaces and their adjacent buildings
Construct buildings continuously all the way to the edge of the path
Make building fronts present slightly irregular angles following the shape of the street

title: PEDESTRIAN DENSITY
summary_en: For any crowd-attracting public space including public plazas, courtyards, pedestrian streets and other gathering venues, first estimate the average number of people P present in the site at any given moment, then set the site area to a range between 150P and 300P square feet. The perceived vibrancy of a pedestrian area is determined by the interrelationship of three variables: the number of people occupying the space, the physical size of the site, and people's subjective perception of its vitality.

numbers_en.v: Estimate average number of people P
numbers_en.k: First estimate the average number of people P present in the site at any given moment
Set the site area to fall between 150P and 300P square feet

numbers_en.v: Oversized space feels desolate and lifeless
numbers_en.k: Excessively large sites spread the crowd thin, so even a large number of people will make the space feel desolate and lifeless

title: ACTIVITY POCKETS
summary_en: Surround the public gathering space with a ring of ACTIVITY POCKETS: these are small, semi-enclosed areas located at the perimeter, protruding toward the open space between circulation paths, and hosting a range of activities that naturally draw people to stop and participate. People are innately inclined to gather at the edges of public space rather than linger in unobstructed open areas. If the perimeter does not provide destinations that support spontaneous lingering, the space will become functionally inactive.

numbers_en.v: Activity pockets distributed along the perimeter
numbers_en.k: Surround public gathering space with a ring of ACTIVITY POCKETS

numbers_en.v: Semi-enclosed, protruding inward toward open space
numbers_en.k: Small, semi-enclosed areas located at the perimeter, protruding toward open space

numbers_en.v: Contain activities to attract people to stay
numbers_en.k: Host internal activities that naturally prompt people to stop and participate

title: STAIR SEATS
summary_en: In any public space where people linger, add a few steps at its edges where stairs descend or elevation changes. Design these raised STAIR SEATS zones to be directly accessible from below, so people can gather and sit on them to observe surrounding activities. This addresses two concurrent user demands: (1) people seek an elevated vantage point that offers a full overview of the entire space, and (2) they want to be part of the scene rather than remaining detached onlookers.

numbers_en.v: Add a few steps at the edge
numbers_en.k: Add a few steps at the edges of areas where people linger and locations with elevation changes
Design the raised areas to be directly accessible from below
Allow people to gather and sit on the structure to watch activities in the surrounding area

title: SOMETHING ROUGHLY IN THE MIDDLE
summary_en: Between the natural pedestrian paths that traverse a public square, courtyard, or public open space, deploy the "SOMETHING ROUGHLY IN THE MIDDLE" arrangement for a selected feature, which may be a fountain, a tree, a statue, a seating-integrated clock tower, a windmill, or a bandstand. This element shall generate a strong, steady spatial pulse for the square that draws people toward its central area. Locate the feature at its natural, appropriate position between the paths, and resist the design impulse to force it to sit exactly at the geometric dead center of the space.

numbers_en.v: Select one feature to place between intersecting paths
numbers_en.k: Select one element to position roughly in the middle of the natural pedestrian paths that traverse the public square

numbers_en.v: Impart a stable pulse to the square
numbers_en.k: Elements including fountains, trees, statues, seating-equipped clock towers, windmills, and bandstands create a consistent spatial pulse for the square and draw people toward its center
Position the element at its natural intended location between paths, do not deliberately place it at the absolute geometric center of the square

title: INTIMACY GRADIENT
summary_en: Arrange all spaces within a building to form a sequential flow: starting from the entrance and the building’s most public section, leading to slightly more private areas, and finally reaching the most private domain. For any building type including residences, offices, public buildings, and summer cottages, occupants require an INTIMACY GRADIENT composed of spaces with varying degrees of privacy. Bedrooms or private chambers are the most private, with rear living rooms as the next tier of privacy.

numbers_en.k: Arrange all spaces of a building into a sequence
Proceed from the most public entrance, through moderately private areas, to the most private domain
People require a gradient consisting of spaces with different levels of privacy

title: INDOOR SUNLIGHT
summary_en: Arrange the most important rooms along the southern edge of the building, and extend the full building along the east-west axis. Conduct fine adjustments to orient appropriate rooms toward southeast and southwest sunlight respectively: for example, public areas are assigned full south-facing exposure, bedrooms face southeast, and porches face southwest. For most climate zones, this design yields an east-west elongated building form consistent with standard INDOOR SUNLIGHT specifications.

numbers_en.v: Key rooms positioned along southern edge
numbers_en.k: Arrange the most important rooms along the southern edge of the building
Extend the building along the east-west axis
Public areas full south-facing, bedrooms southeast, porches southwest

title: COMMON AREAS AT THE HEART
summary_en: Create a single dedicated common area for every social group. Place this area at the centroid of the full space occupied by the group, and configure all ingress and egress paths for the building to be tangent to this common area. Any building that accommodates a social group can only support the routine, unplanned casual encounters between group members when it provides a common area that follows the COMMON AREAS AT THE HEART specification.

numbers_en.k: Create one single common area for each social group
Position at the centroid of the total space occupied by the group

numbers_en.v: Paths tangent to the common area
numbers_en.k: Ensure all building ingress and egress paths are tangent to the space, with all passing routes leading directly into it

title: ENTRANCE ROOM
summary_en: At the main entrance of the building, create a light-filled ENTRANCE ROOM that marks the entrance and straddles the boundary between interior and exterior, covering a portion of outdoor space and a portion of indoor space. Its outdoor portion can function like a traditional old-style porch, while its indoor portion resembles a foyer or living room. The most intuitive description is that the moment of arrival or departure feels as if it expands and dilates, relative to the seconds immediately before and after it.

numbers_en.k: Construct a light-filled room at the main entrance to mark the entry
Straddles the boundary between indoor and outdoor spaces, covering part of the outdoor area and part of the indoor area
The outdoor half resembles an old-style porch, the indoor half resembles a foyer or living room

title: THE FLOW THROUGH ROOMS
summary_en: Avoid corridors and circulation passages as much as possible. Instead, treat public and shared rooms themselves as spaces for both pedestrian movement and gathering, arrange these public rooms in a chain or loop to allow people to move directly from one room to another, and set private rooms to open directly off these public spaces. Ensure all inter-room indoor circulation feels fully unrushed, with one wide, generous circulation path wrapping around the entire residence.

numbers_en.k: Avoid corridors and circulation passages to the greatest possible extent

numbers_en.v: Public rooms function as circulation routes
numbers_en.k: Treat public rooms themselves as spaces for pedestrian movement and gathering

numbers_en.v: Arranged in chain or loop form
numbers_en.k: Arrange public rooms in a chain or loop, with private rooms opening directly onto them

title: SHORT PASSAGES
summary_en: Keep SHORT PASSAGES short. As far as possible, finish them to the standard of occupied rooms, with carpet or wood flooring, furniture, bookshelves, and attractive windows. Design their forms to be open and uncramped, and always provide them with ample light; the highest-quality corridors and passages have windows spanning their entire wall surface. In fact, the ugly, overlong, monotonous corridors of the machine age have already tarnished the reputation of the corridor typology itself.

numbers_en.k: require passages to maintain compact length
lay carpet or wood flooring, and furnish with furniture, bookshelves and attractive windows

numbers_en.v: have generous proportions and sufficient light
numbers_en.k: feature relaxed, unconstrained forms, ample lighting, and ideally full-wall window openings

title: STAIRCASE AS A STAGE
summary_en: Place the main staircase in a critical, highly visible position, and treat the entire flight of stairs as a single room (or as a courtyard if the staircase is located outdoors). Integrate the staircase seamlessly with the adjacent room, arranging it to spiral down along one or two of the room’s walls. Widen the treads at the base of the staircase, so that people descending the stairs are already part of the activities unfolding in the room while still on the stair, and people at the lower level naturally treat the steps as informal seating.

numbers_en.k: Treat the entire flight of stairs as a single room and integrate it fully with the adjacent room
Arrange the staircase to spiral down along one or two of the room’s walls
Widen treads at the staircase base, so people on the stairs become part of indoor activities, and people at the lower level use the steps as seats

title: ZEN VIEW
summary_en: If a site boasts a beautiful scenic view, do not ruin it by installing oversized windows to unreservedly and endlessly take in the entire vista. Instead, place windows oriented toward the view in transitional spaces: along pedestrian paths, in corridors, lobbies, on staircases, and between adjacent rooms. When these view windows are properly positioned, people will catch a fleeting, breathtaking glimpse of the distant landscape as they pass by, and the view remains perpetually captivating exactly because it is only a brief glance.

numbers_en.v: Do not use large windows to greedily take in the full view
numbers_en.k: Do not spoil the beautiful scenic view by using oversized windows to endlessly and greedily consume the vista

numbers_en.v: Locate view windows in transitional spaces
numbers_en.k: Place scenic view windows at transitional positions: along paths, in corridors, lobbies, on staircases, and between rooms

numbers_en.v: Catch a glimpse of the view while passing through
numbers_en.k: People catch a fleeting breathtaking glance of the distant view as they walk past, which remains consistently moving precisely because of its brevity

title: TAPESTRY OF LIGHT AND DARK
summary_en: Create alternating light and dark zones throughout the entire building, configured so that people naturally move toward light as they access key destinations including seating, entrances, staircases, corridors, and exceptionally well-designed scenic spots, while all other areas are rendered dimmer to reinforce this contrast. Humans are innately phototactic: they travel toward light, and orient their bodies toward light even when at rest. As a result, the most beloved, frequently used, and activity-dense spaces in buildings are exactly locations such as window-side seats, balconies, nooks beside fireplaces, and shaded pergola areas.

numbers_en.k: Create alternating light and dark zones across the entire building

numbers_en.v: Travel toward light by innate tendency
numbers_en.k: Guide people to naturally move toward light when heading to key destinations

numbers_en.v: Dim remaining areas to amplify contrast
numbers_en.k: Render all other zones darker to strengthen the light-dark contrast

title: COUPLE'S REALM
summary_en: Set aside a distinct dedicated section within the residential dwelling, separated from all public areas and all children's bedrooms, to create a private space where the adult couple of the household can stay alone. Equip this space with a convenient, unobstructed access path that allows the couple to retreat into it at any time. This space is the COUPLE'S REALM, a genuine territory that belongs exclusively to the two residents, rather than being merely a standard bedroom.

numbers_en.k: Designate a special separate section within the residential unit

numbers_en.v: Separated from public areas and children's rooms
numbers_en.k: Physically divided from all public zones and every child's bedroom in the home

numbers_en.v: The couple can enjoy private time alone
numbers_en.k: Enable the two adult household members to stay alone in the space, with a convenient access path for them to retreat to the space at any time

title: CHILDREN'S REALM
summary_en: First arrange the small, fully child-exclusive zone: the cluster formed by their beds. Position this CHILDREN'S REALM in a separate location at the rear of the house, so that a continuous play space extends all the way from this bed cluster to the street, functioning almost like a wide band running through the interior. This space can accommodate muddy tracks and scattered toys along its path, sits adjacent to the household rooms children need most, especially the bathroom and kitchen, and runs along one side of the common area without disrupting the quiet sections of the home.

numbers_en.k: Prioritize placing the cluster of children's beds in a separate, rear position of the house

numbers_en.v: Continuous play band leading to the street
numbers_en.k: Form a continuous play space extending from the bed cluster to the street

numbers_en.v: Adjacent to bathroom and kitchen, skirting the common area
numbers_en.k: Adjoin the bathroom and kitchen, pass along one side of the common area without disturbing quiet spaces

title: SLEEPING TO THE EAST
summary_en: Orient all sleeping areas within a dwelling to face east, so that occupants wake up in step with rising sun and morning light. This SLEEPING TO THE EAST arrangement usually places sleeping zones on the eastern side of the house, but sleeping areas can also be located on the west side as long as a courtyard or terrace sits to their east. Many people interpret this pattern as a suggestion to crowd all bedrooms to one side of the home, but the core priority is to receive morning light immediately upon waking.

numbers_en.k: Orient the parts of the house intended for sleeping to face east
Enable occupants to wake up together with sunlight and morning light

numbers_en.v: West-side sleeping areas must have a courtyard to their east
numbers_en.k: If the sleeping area is on the west side, a courtyard or terrace must be located to its east

title: FARMHOUSE KITCHEN
summary_en: Make the kitchen larger than typical residential kitchens, sufficiently spacious to fully integrate the program of a family living room, and locate it near the center of the home’s public area rather than tucking it deep at the rear of the house as conventional kitchens are. The space is sized to accommodate a large full table surrounded by a mix of soft upholstered and hard chairs, with work countertops, stoves, and sinks arranged along the room’s perimeter. This layout forms the bright, comfortable space characteristic of the FARMHOUSE KITCHEN pattern.

numbers_en.k: Size the kitchen larger than usual, with sufficient area to accommodate the family living space

numbers_en.v: Near the center of the public zone
numbers_en.k: Position near the core of the public area, rather than being tucked deep at the rear of the house

numbers_en.v: Large table at center, work surfaces along perimeter
numbers_en.k: Able to fit a large table and mix of soft and hard chairs, with countertops, stoves and sinks arranged along the room’s edges

title: PRIVATE TERRACE ON THE STREET
summary_en: Open the common room onto a wide, street-facing terrace or porch, forming the PRIVATE TERRACE ON THE STREET. Slightly elevate the terrace above street level, and border it with a low wall that is short enough for people sitting adjacent to see over it toward the street, yet tall enough to block passersby on the street from peering into the common room. Human nature contains inherent tendencies toward both social interaction and solitude, and a well-designed house supports both types of experience.

numbers_en.v: Common room opens onto the terrace
numbers_en.k: Open the common room onto a wide street-facing terrace or porch
Raise the terrace slightly above the street surface

numbers_en.v: Low wall allows outward views while preventing inward peeking
numbers_en.k: Low wall is short enough for seated people to see outward over it, and tall enough to block people on the street from looking into the house

title: A ROOM OF ONE'S OWN
summary_en: Assign every household member, particularly adult members, a dedicated A ROOM OF ONE'S OWN. The smallest iteration of this private space is a recessed niche fitted with a desk, shelves, and a curtain, while the largest can be a fully independent small room such as a studio or workshop. All such spaces, especially those designated for adults, shall be positioned at the far end of the intimacy gradient, set apart from communal rooms.

numbers_en.k: Assign each household member, especially adults, a dedicated A ROOM OF ONE'S OWN

numbers_en.v: Minimum form is a recessed niche
numbers_en.k: Smallest unit: recessed niche equipped with a desk, shelves and a curtain

numbers_en.v: Placed at the farthest end of the gradient
numbers_en.k: Positioned at the far end of the intimacy gradient, away from communal rooms

title: SEQUENCE OF SITTING SPACES
summary_en: A SEQUENCE OF SITTING SPACES with varying degrees of enclosure is distributed across the entire building. The most formal seating areas are fully enclosed to form independent separate rooms, while the most casual seating areas are placed in the corners of other rooms without any surrounding barriers. The intermediate seating areas are surrounded by partial enclosures, so they remain connected to a larger adjacent space while retaining a certain degree of independence.

numbers_en.v: Hierarchically graded sequence of sitting spaces
numbers_en.k: Arrange a hierarchically graded sequence of sitting spaces throughout the entire building

numbers_en.v: Most formal fully enclosed seating spaces
numbers_en.k: The most formal seating spaces are fully enclosed and set up as independent separate rooms

numbers_en.v: Most casual seating in room corners
numbers_en.k: The most casual seating spaces are placed in the corners of other rooms with no surrounding barriers; intermediate seating spaces are partially enclosed

title: BED CLUSTER
summary_en: Place children’s beds in recessed niches or small niche-like rooms arranged around a shared play space. Each niche is sized sufficiently to fit a small table, a chair, or several tiers of shelves, with at least a small section of floor space reserved for each child to store their personal belongings. Hang curtains at the opening of each niche facing the shared space instead of installing full walls or doors, as solid partitions would overly isolate each bed from the common area.

numbers_en.v: Beds placed in recessed niches surrounding the play space
numbers_en.k: Place children’s beds in niches arranged around a shared play space

numbers_en.v: Dedicated personal space inside each niche
numbers_en.k: Each niche can accommodate a small table, chair or shelves, with reserved floor space for storing personal items

numbers_en.v: Curtains installed instead of walls and doors
numbers_en.k: Hang curtains at niche openings facing the shared space, do not use walls or doors

title: BATHING ROOM
summary_en: Cluster the toilet, shower, washbasin and bathing fixtures in a single tiled area. Site this BATHING ROOM adjacent to the couple’s private domain, with a private access path positioned halfway between the home’s secluded private section and public zones. Where feasible, arrange direct access to the outdoors, leading to a small balcony or enclosed walled courtyard, and install a large bathtub sized to fully submerge at least two people.

numbers_en.v: All fixtures concentrated in one tiled zone
numbers_en.k: Cluster bathing, toilet, shower and washbasin fixtures in a single tiled area

numbers_en.v: Adjacent to couple’s domain, located at midpoint
numbers_en.k: Adjacent to the couple’s private domain with private access, positioned between secluded private areas and public zones

numbers_en.v: Outdoor access available, large bathtub installed
numbers_en.k: Provide access to a small balcony or walled small courtyard if possible; install a bathtub large enough to fully submerge two people

title: BULK STORAGE
summary_en: Do not defer consideration of BULK STORAGE to the final design stage, nor overlook it entirely. Integrate a dedicated full volume for BULK STORAGE within the building, whose floor area accounts for no less than 15% to 20% of the building's total gross floor area. Situate this storage volume in a section of the building with lower construction costs, as it does not require any elaborate fine finishes.

numbers_en.v: Do not defer to the final stage
numbers_en.k: Do not defer consideration of BULK STORAGE to the final design stage or omit it entirely
The BULK STORAGE volume makes up no less than 15% to 20% of the building's total gross floor area
Position the BULK STORAGE volume in a lower construction cost area — it does not require fine finishes

title: FLEXIBLE OFFICE SPACE
summary_en: Arrange the FLEXIBLE OFFICE SPACE as a series of open "wings", with freestanding columns erected along the edges to demarcate interconnected semi-private and public spaces. Deploy a sufficiently large number of columns, so that users can infill the bays between columns in many different semi-permanent configurations over subsequent years. If the target working group is identified before construction, the space can be further tailored to match their specific use needs.

numbers_en.k: arrange the office space into a series of open wings
place freestanding columns along edges to define and interconnect semi-private and public spaces
a sufficient number of columns allow users to infill bays in multiple semi-permanent ways over time

title: COMMUNAL EATING
summary_en: Provide every institution and social group with a space where people can eat together, to make COMMUNAL EATING a regular, normalized practice. Prioritize setting up shared lunch programs at all workplaces, so that a proper full meal consumed around a shared dining table (rather than food taken from boxes, vending machines or paper bags) becomes an important, comfortable daily routine that also leaves room for hosting guests. Our own working group found that this practice operates most successfully when participants take turns preparing meals.

numbers_en.k: Provide every institution and social group with a space for communal eating

numbers_en.v: Communal eating as a normalized routine
numbers_en.k: Make communal eating a regular practice, with a specific focus on rolling out shared lunch programs at all workplaces
A proper full meal eaten around a shared table rather than pre-packaged convenience food, with reserved space for hosting guests

title: SMALL WORK GROUPS
summary_en: Decompose the organization into spatially identifiable SMALL WORK GROUPS, each with fewer than six people. Arrange these groups such that every person can at least partially see other members of their own group, and several groups are organized to share a common entrance, catering, office equipment, drinking water points, and restrooms. In fact, people will feel oppressed whether they work in an undifferentiated crowd or are isolated to work alone.

numbers_en.k: Decompose the organization into spatially identifiable small work groups, with fewer than 6 people per group
Each person can at least partially see other members of their own group
Several groups share entrances, catering, office equipment, drinking water points and restrooms

title: RECEPTION WELCOMES YOU
summary_en: Immediately inside the entrance, arrange a series of welcoming elements: soft chairs, a hearth, food, and coffee. The reception desk is positioned not to span the space between reception staff and the welcome zone, but offset to one side. This configuration allows reception personnel to stand up, walk toward incoming visitors to greet them, and invite them to take a seat.

numbers_en.k: Arrange soft chairs, hearth, food and coffee immediately inside the entrance
Reception desk is not placed across the space between reception staff and the welcome zone
Position the desk offset to one side to enable reception staff to stand up to greet arriving visitors and invite them to sit down

title: A PLACE TO WAIT
summary_en: Create a scenario that turns waiting into a positive experience at sites where people inevitably have to wait, including bus stops, meeting appointment points, and airport terminals. Integrate waiting with a range of other activities such as reading newspapers, drinking coffee, playing billiards, and playing horseshoes, to attract people who are not in a waiting state. Meanwhile, develop a contrasting dedicated space that guides waiting people into contemplation, defined by a calm, positive form of silence.

numbers_en.k: Turn waiting into a positive activity at locations where people are obliged to wait
Combine waiting with activities such as reading newspapers, drinking coffee, and playing billiards to attract people who are not waiting for a scheduled event
Simultaneously create a quiet space that invites contemplation, delivering a state of positive silence

title: SMALL MEETING ROOMS
summary_en: Ensure that no less than 70% of all meeting rooms are designed as SMALL MEETING ROOMS that accommodate 12 people or fewer. Place these rooms in the most public zones of the building, evenly distributed across and between all work areas. The size of a group affects both the number of people who never speak during discussions, and the number of people who hold ideas they never get the opportunity to voice.

numbers_en.k: At least 70% of all meeting rooms are designed to be small
Each room accommodates 12 people or fewer
Located in the most public sections of the building, evenly spread across all work areas

title: HALF-PRIVATE OFFICE
summary_en: Avoid enclosed, separate or private offices. Design every studio, whether intended for two to three people or a single occupant, to be partially open to other work teams and the space outside its boundaries as a HALF-PRIVATE OFFICE. Arrange comfortable seating areas at the front immediately inside the entry, while placing actual work surfaces further inward, set back away from the door. Fully private offices have a devastating impact on the flow of interpersonal interaction in work scenarios.

numbers_en.k: Avoid enclosed, separate or private offices
Each studio is half-open to adjacent work teams and the external space
Arrange comfortable seating at the front inside the entrance, set work surfaces further inward away from the door

title: ROOMS TO RENT
summary_en: Designate at least one portion of the residential building as rentable space: in addition to its regular internal connection to the rest of the dwelling, provide this space with an independent private entrance. Ensure that the regular connecting access can be easily sealed off without disrupting the internal circulation of the main home, and that occupants can reach a bathroom directly from this rentable room without traversing the main residential unit. This straightforward spatial arrangement allows the space to be adjusted accordingly when a household or work group shrinks due to the departure of one or two members.

numbers_en.k: Make at least part of the building rentable
Provide an additional private entrance outside the regular internal connection

numbers_en.v: Sealable internal door, direct bathroom access
numbers_en.k: The regular entrance can be easily sealed, and the bathroom is directly accessible without passing through the main dwelling

title: TEENAGER'S COTTAGE
summary_en: To mark a child’s coming of age, their allocated space within the family home is converted into a TEENAGER'S COTTAGE, which materially expresses the start of their independent life. This unit remains attached to the main residential structure, but is designed as a clearly visible protruding volume, sited away from the master bedroom, with its own private entrance and potentially its own separate roof. In the majority of family dwellings, rooms assigned to children and teenagers are essentially identical in nature, a situation that is not supposed to be the case.

numbers_en.k: Convert the child’s designated space in the family home into a cottage to mark their coming of age

numbers_en.v: Clearly protruding, located away from the master bedroom
numbers_en.k: Remain attached to the main dwelling while forming a clearly visible protruding volume, set apart from the master bedroom

numbers_en.v: Independent private entrance and separate roof
numbers_en.k: Equipped with its own private entrance, and potentially its own independent roof

title: OLD AGE COTTAGE
summary_en: OLD AGE COTTAGE are purpose-built units constructed specifically for older adults. A subset of these units are sited on the grounds of larger primary residences to house elderly grandparents, while the rest are situated on fully independent parcels that are far smaller than standard residential homestead plots. All such OLD AGE COTTAGE are positioned at ground level, directly adjacent to the street along regularly used pedestrian routes, and in close proximity to all neighborhood services and public land.

numbers_en.k: Purpose-built cottages exclusively for the elderly

numbers_en.v: Located within large residential lots or on small independent parcels
numbers_en.k: Some sited on larger residential lots for grandparent occupancy, others on independent parcels far smaller than standard plots

numbers_en.v: Ground-floor location, street frontage, adjacent to services
numbers_en.k: All placed at ground level, directly adjacent to pedestrian street frontages, close to neighborhood services and public land

title: SETTLED WORK
summary_en: Give every person, especially as they grow older, the opportunity to establish their own workspace inside their home or directly adjacent to their residence. Design this space to support gradual growth: it may initially only support a weekend hobby, and slowly evolve into a full, productive, comfortable workshop. The concept of SETTLED WORK weaves all distinct threads of an individual's life into a single, dynamic working practice.
