numbers_en.k: Opportunity for every person (especially as they age) to establish their own workspace

numbers_en.v: Located inside the home or immediately adjacent to the home
numbers_en.k: Workspace sited within one's own home or directly next to the home
Start from a weekend hobby, gradually develop into a complete, productive, comfortable workshop

title: HOME WORKSHOP
summary_en: Carve out a dedicated space for productive work within a residential unit, using the space not merely for casual hobbies but as a site of formal livelihood operation. Revise zoning regulations to encourage small-scale, low-noise production activities to operate within residential districts. Allocate several hundred square feet of floor area for this HOME WORKSHOP, and position its frontage to be visible from the public street, so that the owner may hang their official business sign.

numbers_en.v: Space for productive work in the home
numbers_en.k: Carve out a space for productive work in the home, which functions as a livelihood rather than only a hobby

numbers_en.v: Revise regulations to accommodate small operations
numbers_en.k: Amend zoning regulations to encourage quiet, small-scale operations to locate in residential areas

numbers_en.v: Several hundred square feet, visible from the street
numbers_en.k: Allocate several hundred square feet of space for it, make it visible from the street, and allow the display of business signage

title: OPEN STAIRS
summary_en: Eliminate enclosed internal stairwells within institutional facilities to the greatest extent possible, and directly connect all autonomous households, public services, and work groups located on the building’s upper floors to the ground level. This is achieved by constructing OPEN STAIRS that run directly upward from the street: whether the stairs are fitted with a roof is determined by local climatic conditions, but in all cases, the stairs must remain open at ground level with no doors installed, making the stair functionally a continuation of the street. No upper-floor corridors shall be constructed.

numbers_en.k: Eliminate internal stairwells inside institutional premises to the maximum possible extent

numbers_en.v: Upper floors directly connected to ground level
numbers_en.k: All autonomous households, services and work groups on upper floors are directly connected to the ground

numbers_en.v: Stair base is open with no doors
numbers_en.k: Stairs remain open at ground level with no doors installed, functioning as a continuation of the street; no upper-floor corridors are constructed

title: LIGHT ON TWO SIDES OF EVERY ROOM
summary_en: Arrange every room such that it abuts outdoor space on at least two sides, then install windows on both of these exterior walls to allow natural light to enter each room from more than one direction. This design rule, corresponding to the formal pattern LIGHT ON TWO SIDES OF EVERY ROOM, arguably determines the success or failure of a room more than any other single pattern. The distribution of daylight within a room and the presence of windows on two separate exterior facades are the core critical factors that define the performance of the space.

numbers_en.v: abut outdoor space on at least two sides
numbers_en.k: Arrange every room to abut outdoor space on at least two sides

numbers_en.v: install windows on two exterior walls
numbers_en.k: Install windows on these two exterior walls

numbers_en.v: natural light enters from multiple directions
numbers_en.k: Enable natural light to enter every room from more than one direction

title: BUILDING EDGE
summary_en: Treat the BUILDING EDGE strictly as an object, a place, and a volumetric zone, rather than a dimensionless line or interface. Design the BUILDING EDGE with crenellation-like indentations and protrusions, populated with spaces that invite people to pause. Create recessed, covered spaces that support sitting, leaning, and walking, especially at perimeter locations that overlook interesting outdoor public life.

numbers_en.v: The BUILDING EDGE is a volumetric zone
numbers_en.k: Treat the edge as an object, a place, and a volumetric zone
Design the BUILDING EDGE with alternating indentations and protrusions, filled with spaces that invite people to stay
Create recessed, covered spaces that support sitting, leaning, and walking

title: SUNNY PLACE
summary_en: On a south-facing yard, garden or site, locate the point with the best solar exposure between the building and the outdoor area. Develop this point into a distinct SUNNY PLACE, a vital outdoor room that can serve as a sunlit work space, a spot fitted with swings and special landscape plants, or a dedicated area for sun exposure. Be certain to place this SUNNY PLACE in a wind-sheltered position, as year-round prevailing winds will make this otherwise most desirable space unfit for use.

numbers_en.k: Identify the point with the best solar access between the building and outdoor space in a south-facing courtyard
Develop into a dedicated SUNNY PLACE, a key outdoor room
Site in a wind-protected location — prevailing year-round winds will leave the most desirable space unused

title: NORTH FACE
summary_en: Design the building's NORTH FACE as a series of cascading, tiered steps that slope down toward the ground, so sunlight that would otherwise cast a long shadow on the building's north side can reach the ground immediately adjacent to the structure. A building with a steep, vertical north facade will cast an extended shadow behind it for many months of the year. These lifeless, gloomy north-facing zones not only waste large tracts of land, but also fragment the surrounding environment with uninviting shadow belts that no one is willing to traverse.

numbers_en.k: Form the building's north face as a series of cascading tiered steps sloping down to the ground

numbers_en.v: Sunlight reaches the building's base perimeter
numbers_en.k: Enable sunlight to fall on the ground immediately adjacent to the building
Prevent steep vertical north facades from casting long trailing shadows that waste land and fragment the surrounding environment

title: OUTDOOR ROOM
summary_en: Construct a highly enclosed open-air space that, while remaining open to the sky, delivers the experiential quality of an interior room, which is the core design logic of the OUTDOOR ROOM pattern. To achieve this effect, delineate the space by setting columns at each of its corners, and optionally add partial overhead covering with a pergola or retractable canvas. Form the perimeter "walls" of the space using fences, sitting low walls, screens, hedges, or the exterior walls of adjacent buildings.

numbers_en.k: Enclose sufficiently so that the space feels like a room even though it is open to the sky
Delineate the space using columns placed at every corner

numbers_en.v: Partially covered top, walls on all four sides
numbers_en.k: Partially cover the top with a pergola or retractable canvas; use fences, low walls, screens, hedges or exterior building walls as the "walls"

title: STREET WINDOWS
summary_en: Where buildings extend along busy streets, incorporate STREET WINDOWS with built-in window seats that face outward toward the street. Place these windows in bedrooms, or at points on corridors and staircases that are consistently passed by people. At the ground floor level, set the sills of these windows high enough to maintain interior privacy. These street-facing windows provide a unique connection between the life inside the building and the public street.

numbers_en.k: Install STREET WINDOWS with window seats facing outward toward the street at all locations where buildings run along busy streets
Positioned in bedrooms, or at points on corridors and staircases that are constantly traversed by passersby

numbers_en.v: Elevated on ground floor for privacy
numbers_en.k: These windows on the ground floor must be set sufficiently high to preserve privacy

title: OPENING TO THE STREET
summary_en: Any public space whose success or failure hinges on proper implementation of the OPENING TO THE STREET design must be opened up using a full wall that can be completely pushed open. Where possible, arrange a portion of its activities on the opposite side of the sidewalk, so that the space truly spans the pedestrian path, and people passing along the street will move directly through the space as they traverse the walkway. There are dozens of distinct methods to construct such an opening.

numbers_en.v: The entire wall can be fully opened
numbers_en.k: Open the space using a full wall that can be completely pushed open

numbers_en.v: Activities extend across to the other side of the sidewalk
numbers_en.k: If possible, place a portion of activities on the opposite side of the sidewalk
Make the space span the pedestrian path, so that people passing along the road walk through it

title: GALLERY SURROUND
summary_en: Wherever feasible, construct porches, gallery platforms, arcades, balconies, recessed niches, outdoor seating, awnings, and pergola rooms along the building edge of every floor, particularly where these elements open onto public spaces and streets, and connect them directly to internal rooms with doors. Following the GALLERY SURROUND principle, this design transforms the building perimeter on every level into a fully habitable zone, rather than only a passive, uninhabited exterior shell.

numbers_en.k: Construct along the building edge of every floor wherever possible

numbers_en.v: Gallery platforms, balconies, recessed niches, awnings
numbers_en.k: Porches, gallery platforms, arcades, balconies, recessed niches, outdoor seating, awnings, pergola rooms

numbers_en.v: Directly connect to interior rooms via doors
numbers_en.k: Use doors to connect these elements directly to internal rooms

title: SIX-FOOT BALCONY
summary_en: Whenever you build a balcony, porch, loggia, or terrace, make it at least six feet deep. If possible, recess at least a portion of it into the building, so that it is not cantilevered out and separated from the building by a simple line, and partially enclose it. Balconies and porches are often made very small to save costs, but when they are too small, constructing them delivers no practical functional value equivalent to completing the feature.

numbers_en.k: All balconies, porches, loggias and terraces shall have a minimum depth of six feet
Where possible, recess a portion of the feature into the building instead of simply cantilevering it outward
Partially enclose the feature

title: CONNECTION TO THE EARTH
summary_en: Construct a series of paths, terraces and steps along the edge of the building to form the CONNECTION TO THE EARTH between the structure and its surrounding land. These elements are intentionally positioned to blur the distinct boundary between building and ground, to the point that it is impossible to clearly demarcate where the building ends and the earth begins. The best way to grasp this design logic is to compare buildings that are completely severed from the adjacent land with those that maintain full spatial continuity with the ground.

numbers_en.k: Construct a series of paths, terraces and steps along the edge of the building
Intentionally arrange these elements to blur the boundary between the building and the land

numbers_en.v: cannot clearly identify the boundary location
numbers_en.k: Make it impossible to clearly define where the building ends and the earth begins

title: TERRACED SLOPE
summary_en: On all sloped land, including fields, parks, public gardens, and even private gardens surrounding residential properties, a set of terraces and earth ridges running along contour lines is implemented to form the TERRACED SLOPE. The construction method involves building low walls along the contour lines, then backfilling soil behind these walls to form level terraces. Buildings do not need to be adjusted to accommodate these terraces, and can fully extend unobstructed across them.

numbers_en.v: Construct terraces on all sloped land
numbers_en.k: A set of terraces and earth ridges is built on all sloped land
Terraces and earth ridges are aligned along contour lines
Low walls are built along contour lines, then backfilled with soil to form terraces

title: FRUIT TREES
summary_en: Plant small, scattered FRUIT TREES orchards in gardens, on public lands along paths and streets, in parks, and across residential neighborhoods, at every site where a well-established local community group exists that is capable of independently tending to the trees and harvesting their fruit. The seasonal, fruit-bearing nature of fruit trees produces unique distinct outcomes: the presence of these orchards reintroduces an experience that has nearly vanished from cities, the firsthand experience of organic growth.

numbers_en.k: Plant small-scale orchards across gardens, public lands, parks and neighborhoods

numbers_en.v: Along paths, streets and public lands
numbers_en.k: Public lands along paths and streets, parks, and residential neighborhoods
All locations with established mature local groups that can independently tend the trees and harvest their fruit

title: TREE PLACES
summary_en: When planting trees, follow their inherent natural growth characteristics, arranging them to form enclosures, shaded avenues, quadrangles, tree groves, and large standalone trees that stretch freely toward the middle of open spaces. Adjacent buildings are designed to respond to these tree layouts, so that the trees themselves, as well as the combined configurations of trees and buildings, form usable TREE PLACES for people.

numbers_en.k: Plant trees in accordance with the trees' own inherent natural growth habits

numbers_en.v: Enclosure / Avenue / Quadrangle / Grove / Standalone Tree
numbers_en.k: Form enclosures, shaded avenues, quadrangles, groves, and freely extending standalone large trees
Adjacent buildings are shaped to respond to trees, jointly creating usable places with trees

title: GARDEN GROWING WILD
summary_en: Allow grasses, mosses, shrubs, flowers and trees to grow in a manner close to their natural state, intermingled and intertwined without any partitions, leaving no exposed bare soil and no formal geometric flower beds. All boundaries and edging details are constructed from rough stone, brick and timber, making them an integral part of the naturally growing landscape. Many gardens are overly formal and artificial, with planting beds trimmed to be as neat and uniform as tablecloths or oil paintings.

numbers_en.k: Grow grasses, mosses, shrubs, flowers and trees in a near-natural manner

numbers_en.v: Intermingled growth, no partitions, no bare soil
numbers_en.k: Intermingle and grow intertwined, with no partitions, no exposed bare soil, and no formal structured flower beds

numbers_en.v: Edging constructed from rough stone, brick and wood
numbers_en.k: All boundaries and edging are made of rough stone, brick and wood to form part of the natural growth

title: GARDEN WALL
summary_en: Create a certain type of enclosure to protect the interior of a quiet garden from the sight and noise of passing traffic. For large gardens or parks, this enclosure can be soft, and may incorporate shrubs, trees, gentle slopes and other elements. However, the smaller the garden, the more rigid and definite its enclosure must be; in a very small garden, the enclosure must be formed by buildings or GARDEN WALLs, as even hedges and fences are not sufficient to block out sound.

numbers_en.v: Construct enclosure to block traffic sight and noise
numbers_en.k: Create enclosure to protect the garden interior from the sight and noise of passing traffic
Enclosure for large gardens or parks can be soft, including shrubs, trees, gentle slopes
The smaller the garden, the more rigid its enclosure must be: extremely small gardens require buildings or walls, as hedges and fences cannot block noise

title: TRELLISED WALK
summary_en: Where a path requires special shelter or a degree of privacy, a trellis is erected over the path and fully planted with climbing flowering plants to form a TRELLISED WALK. This floral trellis structure is used to help shape the outdoor spaces on both of its sides.

numbers_en.v: Erect trellis over path and plant climbing flowers
numbers_en.k: Erect a trellis over paths that require shelter or privacy, and fully plant the trellis with climbing flowering plants
All locations where a path requires special shelter or a certain measure of privacy
Use this floral trellis to help shape the outdoor spaces on its two sides

title: GREENHOUSE
summary_en: In temperate climates, integrate the greenhouse as an integral part of your residence or workplace, such that it acts both as a room of the building that is directly accessible without stepping outside, and as a component of the adjacent garden that can be entered directly from the garden. Envision a simple greenhouse attached to the side of a living room, oriented to face winter sunlight and fitted with shelves for growing flowers and vegetables, with a door leading into the interior of the home for convenient entry and use.

numbers_en.v: Constructed as part of the residence
numbers_en.k: Integrate the greenhouse as part of a residence or workplace in temperate climates

numbers_en.v: Functions as one interior room of the house
numbers_en.k: Serves as a room of the house that can be accessed directly without going outdoors

numbers_en.v: Functions as one space within the garden
numbers_en.k: Serves as a part of the garden that can be entered directly from the garden

title: GARDEN SEAT
summary_en: Create a quiet spot in the garden: a private enclosed space with a comfortable seat, dense vegetation, and sunlight. Carefully select the placement of the GARDEN SEAT, choosing the location that evokes the strongest sense of solitude. As we have repeatedly noted in this pattern language, the ability to be alone is of profound importance.

numbers_en.k: Create a quiet spot in the garden
A private enclosure with a comfortable seat, dense vegetation, and sunlight
Carefully select the location, pick the spot that brings the strongest sense of solitude

title: VEGETABLE GARDEN
summary_en: Set aside a plot on private garden grounds or public land as a VEGETABLE GARDEN. A family of four needs approximately one-tenth of an acre for this use. The VEGETABLE GARDEN must be sited in a full-sun location, positioned centrally relative to all households it serves, enclosed, and equipped with an adjacent small shed for storing gardening tools, as vegetables are a fundamental food staple.

numbers_en.v: Set aside a plot for use as a vegetable garden
numbers_en.k: Set aside a plot on private garden grounds or public land for use as a vegetable garden

numbers_en.v: Approximately 1/10 acre for a family of four
numbers_en.k: A family of four requires approximately one-tenth of an acre

numbers_en.v: Full-sun location, central positioning, enclosure, and tool shed provision
numbers_en.k: Sited in a full-sun location, positioned at the center of all served households, enclosed, and fitted with an adjacent small gardening tool shed

title: COMPOST
summary_en: Place all toilets above a single dry compost chamber. Route the feed pipes for organic waste to this same chamber, and use the combined product of the two as fertilizer. To urban residents, the sewer system appears to operate flawlessly: it is clean and uncluttered, all waste is removed with a single flush, but this modern system actually flushes away all nutrients that should be returned to the land.

numbers_en.v: Toilets are positioned above the compost chamber
numbers_en.k: Arrange all toilets above a single dry compost chamber

numbers_en.v: Food waste is fed into the same chamber
numbers_en.k: Route the feed pipes for organic waste to the same chamber

numbers_en.v: The combined product is used as fertilizer
numbers_en.k: Use the combined product of the two as fertilizer

title: ALCOVES
summary_en: Along the edges of any public room, create a series of small recessed spaces designated as ALCOVES, which are typically no more than 6 feet in width and 3 to 6 feet in depth, and can be far smaller. These alcoves must be sufficiently large to fit two people sitting to chat or play, and in some cases large enough to hold a desk or small table. This design consideration is most acutely prominent in the public rooms of residential dwellings: kitchens, family rooms, and living rooms.

numbers_en.v: Create small spaces along the edge of public rooms
numbers_en.k: Construct a series of small spaces along the perimeter of any public room
Typically no more than 6 feet wide, 3 to 6 feet deep, and may be considerably smaller

numbers_en.v: Accommodate two people or a small table
numbers_en.k: Large enough to fit two people sitting to chat or play, and sometimes hold a desk or small table

title: WINDOW PLACE
summary_en: In every room you occupy for a period of time during the day, convert at least one window into a WINDOW PLACE. It is easy to dismiss such spaces as unaffordable luxuries that can no longer be constructed or enjoyed. In reality, the issue is far more urgent: windows designed to create a distinct place adjacent to them are the critical determinant of a room's habitability.

numbers_en.v: Implement in every regularly used room
numbers_en.k: Implement in every room that you spend a period of time in during the day
Convert at least one window into a WINDOW PLACE

numbers_en.v: A place rather than a mere opening
numbers_en.k: Create a habitable, occupiable place adjacent to the window, instead of only a viewing opening

title: THE FIRE
summary_en: Place THE FIRE in a shared public space, possibly the kitchen, to make it the natural focal point for conversation, reverie, and contemplation. Adjust its position until it connects all surrounding social spaces and adjacent rooms, ensuring each of these areas has a partial line of sight to the fire, and incorporate a window or other secondary focal element to anchor the character of the space when the fire is unlit. Televisions often serve as a default focal point for rooms, but they are a crude, inauthentic substitute for a truly vibrant, living element that animates the interior.

numbers_en.v: Locate THE FIRE in a public space
numbers_en.k: Place THE FIRE in a public space, potentially the kitchen

numbers_en.v: Connect all surrounding adjacent rooms and social spaces
numbers_en.k: Adjust the position of THE FIRE until it links all surrounding social spaces, so that every area can catch a glimpse of the fire

numbers_en.v: Install a window to anchor the space
numbers_en.k: Set a window or other focal point to sustain the character of the place when THE FIRE is extinguished

title: EATING ATMOSPHERE
summary_en: Place a substantial, sturdy large table at the center of the dining space, sized large enough to accommodate the entire family or the full group of users. Install a lamp above the table to create a distinct pool of light over the gathered group, and enclose this defined zone with walls or contrasting dark unlit space. Dimension the overall space sufficiently to allow chairs to be pulled backward comfortably, and provide adjacent shelves and counter tops to hold all items associated with the meal.

numbers_en.k: Place a sturdy large table at the center of the dining space that can accommodate the entire family or full group of users

numbers_en.v: One pool of light under the overhead lamp
numbers_en.k: Set a lamp above the table to create a pool of light over all people in the group

numbers_en.v: Enclosed by walls or contrasting darkness
numbers_en.k: Enclose this space with walls or contrasting darkness

title: WORKSPACE ENCLOSURE
summary_en: Allocate a minimum of 60 square feet of area to each workspace. Construct walls and install windows around each workspace, such that their total combined area (with windows counted at half their actual area) equals 50% to 75% of the total enclosure area of a fully enclosed 60-square-foot unit with solid walls on all four sides. Keep at least 8 feet of the front edge of the workspace open, with this opening always oriented toward a larger adjacent space, and arrange desks so that working occupants can look outward, either forward or to the side.

numbers_en.k: Allocate a minimum of 60 square feet to each workspace
Total area of walls and windows (windows counted at half their actual area) is 50%–75% of a full solid-wall enclosure

numbers_en.v: minimum 8 feet of front edge open facing a larger space
numbers_en.k: At least 8 feet of the front side is open, and the opening always faces a larger space

title: COOKING LAYOUT
summary_en: To strike a balance between an undersized kitchen and an overly extravagant kitchen, arrange the stove, sink, food storage, and work counter following these COOKING LAYOUT requirements: (1) The distance between any two of the four elements does not exceed 10 feet; (2) The total length of the work counter (excluding the sink, stove top, and refrigerator) is at least 12 feet; (3) No individual segment of the work counter is shorter than 4 feet.

numbers_en.k: Distance between any two of the four elements (stove, sink, food storage, work counter) does not exceed 10 feet
Total length of work counter (excluding sink, stove and refrigerator) is at least 12 feet
No individual work counter segment is shorter than 4 feet

title: SITTING CIRCLE
summary_en: Position every individual seating spot in a protected location that is not traversed by circulation paths or pedestrian movement, arranged in a roughly circular SITTING CIRCLE configuration. Let the room itself subtly imply the boundary of this circle, with paths and activities distributed around its perimeter, so people naturally gravitate toward the chairs when they feel inclined to sit, without the space feeling overly enclosed. Arrange chairs and cushions loosely in a ring, and err on the side of preparing one or two extra seats.

numbers_en.k: Position seating spots in protected locations not traversed by paths or pedestrian movement
Form the SITTING CIRCLE in a roughly circular shape, with the room itself subtly indicating the circle

numbers_en.v: Loose arrangement, prioritize extra seats over insufficient ones
numbers_en.k: Arrange chairs and cushions loosely in a circle, and prepare one or two extra seats

title: COMMUNAL SLEEPING
summary_en: Arrange the sleeping area to allow children and adults the possibility of sleeping in the same shared space, within mutual sight and sound reach, at least as an occasional option outside of their usual sleeping habits. This can be implemented in the communal zone adjacent to the fireplace, where the entire family together with guests can spread a large mat and several blankets in the recessed alcove to achieve the COMMUNAL SLEEPING arrangement.

numbers_en.k: Enable the possibility for children and adults to sleep in the same space

numbers_en.v: Visible and audible to each other
numbers_en.k: Be within each other's sight and sound reach
Serve at minimum as an occasional alternative outside regular sleeping habits

title: MARRIAGE BED
summary_en: At the appropriate stage of a couple’s life, they create a special MARRIAGE BED for themselves that acts as an intimate anchor point in their daily life. The space is slightly enclosed, fitted with a low ceiling or canopy, and designed to support continuous additions to the bed and its surrounding area, so it becomes increasingly personalized and one-of-a-kind as the years pass. Customizable elements that enable this evolution include a headboard that can be carved, painted and repainted, or a fabric canopy that can be replaced and embroidered.

numbers_en.k: make a custom MARRIAGE BED for oneself at the right life stage

numbers_en.v: slightly enclosed, low ceiling or canopy
numbers_en.k: slightly enclosed layout with a low roof or fabric canopy
add elements continuously to make the space more personalized and unique as time passes

references: Homer, Odyssey (Odysseus and Penelope's immovable bed).

title: BED ALCOVE
summary_en: Do not place single beds in empty rooms conventionally labeled as "bedrooms". Instead, carve out individual bed alcoves adjacent to spaces with other non-sleep functions, so that the bed itself forms a small private sanctuary. This pattern is indispensable if you are constructing a very small house no larger than 300 or 400 square feet, especially a property planned for phased expansion at a later stage.

numbers_en.k: Do not place single beds in empty rooms referred to as bedrooms

numbers_en.v: Bed alcoves sited adjacent to multi-functional rooms
numbers_en.k: Locate individual bed alcoves next to rooms with other non-sleep functions
Make the bed itself a small private haven

title: DRESSING ROOM
summary_en: Provide every person with a DRESSING ROOM, either private or shared, situated between their bed and bathroom. Make this DRESSING ROOM large enough to contain an open floor area with a minimum diameter of 6 feet, roughly 6 linear feet of hanging clothing space, an additional approximately 6 linear feet of open shelving, and two to three drawers.

numbers_en.k: Provide each person with a DRESSING ROOM located between the bed and bathroom

numbers_en.v: Open floor area with diameter ≥ 6 feet
numbers_en.k: Contain an open floor area with a minimum diameter of 6 feet

numbers_en.v: 6 ft hanging space + 6 ft open shelving + 2-3 drawers
numbers_en.k: Approximately 6 feet of hanging space, approximately 6 feet of open shelving, and two to three drawers

title: CEILING HEIGHT VARIETY
summary_en: Vary ceiling heights continuously throughout the entire building, particularly between rooms that open directly to one another, so that people can perceive the relative degree of intimacy of different spaces. Specifically, set high ceilings of 10 to 12 feet in public rooms or spaces for large gatherings, use moderately lower ceilings of 7 to 9 feet in rooms for smaller gatherings, and implement very low ceilings in rooms or alcoves designed for one or two people.

numbers_en.k: Enable continuous ceiling height variation, especially between interconnected rooms
Raise ceiling height for public or large gathering rooms (10 to 12 feet)
Lower ceiling height for smaller gathering spaces (7-9 feet), set very low ceiling heights for rooms or alcoves for 1 to 2 people

title: THE SHAPE OF INDOOR SPACE
summary_en: Except for occasional exceptions, every indoor space, or every location within a space, shall be made roughly rectangular per the specification of THE SHAPE OF INDOOR SPACE: walls are approximately straight, wall corners are nearly right angles, and each room is capped with a roughly symmetrical vault (or low-pitch roof). Anomalous space configurations including single-slope shed roofs, sharply elevated pointed roofs, bulges protruding into the room interior, and recessed wall corners shall be avoided. The shape of a room is determined by the social space it accommodates.

numbers_en.k: Make every indoor space a roughly rectangular form

numbers_en.v: Straight walls, right angles, symmetrical roofs
numbers_en.k: Walls are roughly straight, wall corners are nearly right angles, the top is covered with a roughly symmetrical vault or low-slope roof
Avoid single-slope shed roofs, pointed roofs, inward-protruding bulges, and recessed wall corners

title: WINDOWS OVERLOOKING LIFE
summary_en: Position the window of every room to face the most interesting, vibrant outdoor spots, including streets, gardens, and ongoing activities. As defined by the "WINDOWS OVERLOOKING LIFE" design principle, every regularly occupied room shall have at least one window facing a lively, lived-in scene, rather than a blank exterior wall or uninviting dead blind spot. Windows with no view of daily life never prompt people to pause when passing by, while windows that overlook active living scenes effectively connect the indoor space to the dynamic outside world.

numbers_en.k: Place windows to face the most vibrant locations including streets, gardens, activities and other lively spots

numbers_en.v: At least one window overlooking life
numbers_en.k: At least one window in each regularly occupied room faces a lively, lived-in scene

numbers_en.v: Avoid blank walls and dead blind spots
numbers_en.k: Instead of facing blank exterior walls or dead blind spots

title: HALF-OPEN WALL
summary_en: Adjust the walls, openings, and windows of each interior space to strike an appropriate balance between open, flowing spaces and grid-like enclosed compartments. Do not take for granted that every space must be a fully enclosed room, nor that all spaces must be mutually interconnected. The appropriate balance always lies between these two extremes: no room is completely sealed, and no space is fully connected to any other space.

numbers_en.v: Adjust walls, openings and windows for balance
numbers_en.k: Adjust walls, openings and windows to strike a proper balance between openness and enclosure

numbers_en.v: No full enclosure, no full interconnection
numbers_en.k: No room is completely enclosed, and no space is fully connected to another
Achieve this effect using HALF-OPEN WALL elements such as half-height walls, wide openings, and columns

title: INTERIOR WINDOWS
summary_en: Install fully transparent fixed-glass INTERIOR WINDOWS between rooms that feel lifeless due to insufficient internal activity, or are exceptionally dark because of their inward, deep-set location. This configuration is most commonly seen in corridors and aisles, spaces that easily appear completely empty and unoccupied. These INTERIOR WINDOWS strengthen occupants' sense of mutual connection, and the building's internal circulation paths are thus imbued with new vitality.

numbers_en.k: Between rooms that are lifeless due to too little activity or exceptionally dark
Install fully transparent fixed-glass INTERIOR WINDOWS
This scenario is most commonly found in corridors and aisles

title: STAIRCASE VOLUME
summary_en: Create a two-story STAIRCASE VOLUME to house the stair, which may be straight, L-shaped, U-shaped, or C-shaped. Stairs can be as narrow as 2 feet for very steep stair runs, or as wide as 5 feet for spacious, gently graded stairs. Under all circumstances, the entire stair well must form a complete, two-story structural bay, and it is not required for all stairs to follow the so-called "standard" 30-degree angle.

numbers_en.k: Create a two-story through volume to accommodate the stair
It can be straight, L-shaped, U-shaped or C-shaped

numbers_en.v: Full stair well constitutes one complete structural bay
numbers_en.k: The entire stair well must form a complete, two-story structural bay

title: CORNER DOORS
summary_en: Unless there is a specific justified reason to position a door at the center of a wall, place the door at the room's corner following the CORNER DOORS principle. If a room has two doors that serve as through access for people passing across the space, locate both doors close to the same corner. This arrangement allows the through circulation path to skim along one edge of the room, rather than cutting through and severing the central open space.

numbers_en.k: Unless there are special justifications, place doors at the corners of the room

numbers_en.v: Two doors adjacent to the same corner
numbers_en.k: If two doors are provided for through passage, arrange both of them close to the same corner
Make the through movement path skim along one side of the room without severing the central space

title: THICK WALLS
summary_en: Once you have lived in a space for a long time, you will want to adjust the walls around you to better suit your own preferences. For this reason, the THICK WALLS pattern advocates building walls to be thick, solid, and internally modifiable: all areas that can be used, gradually altered, and occupied by occupants are designed as thick walls, with embedded window seats, deep shelves, niches, and even small recessed corners that can be used for sitting or leaning.

title: STRUCTURE FOLLOWS SOCIAL SPACES
summary_en: The first principle of construction is that under no circumstances should the engineering structure dominate architectural form. Load-bearing components including columns, walls and floor slabs shall be arranged in alignment with the social spaces within the building, and social spaces must never be adjusted to accommodate the building's engineering structure. This proper correspondence, however, is almost never achieved in modern construction.

title: EFFICIENT STRUCTURE
summary_en: Conceptualize the building as a monolithic structure built entirely from continuous compression-resistant materials. Geometrically, it is defined as a three-dimensional system consisting of individual vaulted spaces, most of which are roughly rectangular, fitted with thin load-bearing walls. Each wall is stiffened at regular intervals along its length by columns, with thickened sections at the junctions between adjacent walls and between walls and vaults, and additional reinforcement installed around all openings.

title: GOOD MATERIALS
summary_en: Only use biodegradable, low-energy consumption materials that are easy to cut and modify on site. For bulk primary GOOD MATERIALS, we recommend ultra-light 40 to 60 pound concrete, as well as soil-based materials including rammed earth, brick and tile. For secondary GOOD MATERIALS, use wood planks, gypsum, plywood, fabric, wire mesh, paper, cardboard, particle board, corrugated iron, lime plaster, bamboo, rope and tile.

title: GRADUAL STIFFENING
summary_en: Recognize that you are not assembling a building from a batch of components, but tangibly nurturing it to grow into its final form. You first put up a rough frame, then implement GRADUAL STIFFENING step by step: erect columns first, then lay walls, then install the roof, before incrementally thickening and finishing every single structural member. summary_en: Arrange the ROOF LAYOUT such that each distinct individual roof corresponds to a recognizable social unit within the building or building complex. summary_en: Arrange column stiffeners to be spaced farthest apart from one another at the ground floor, with their positions growing progressively closer as you move upward through the building. title: ROOT FOUNDATIONS
summary_en: A viable foundation construction method is explored, where the column itself extends continuously into the ground and spreads out underground, with the material of the footing and the column fully integrated as a single whole. This integrated assembly of the column and its attached footing, defined as ROOT FOUNDATIONS, performs like a tree root, with capacity to resist not only compressive forces, but also tensile forces and horizontal shear forces. When the column and the foundation are two separate components that require secondary connection, that connection joint becomes the weakest structural link.

summary_en: Fabricate BOX COLUMNS as filled hollow tubes, with a stiff tubular outer shell on the exterior and a high compressive strength solid core on the interior. The outer shell is configured to deliver sufficient tensile strength, which can be achieved either through the inherent tensile performance of the shell material itself, or via reinforcing steel wires embedded in the filling material. title: PERIMETER BEAMS
summary_en: Construct a continuous PERIMETER BEAMS loop running the full circumference of the room, engineered to be sufficiently robust to resist the horizontal thrust of the overlying vault, distribute upper-story loads to columns, tie all columns to one another, and serve as lintels across openings in the walls. This perimeter beam is fully integrated as a single monolithic unit with the columns, walls and floor slabs above it, as well as the columns and walls below it. This column-interconnected perimeter beam precedes all other components to form the distinct, perceivable structural volume of the space.

title: WALL MEMBRANE
summary_en: Form the wall as a WALL MEMBRANE that connects columns, door frames and window frames, and is at least partially integrated with these components. To construct such a wall, first erect two inner and outer membrane layers that can function as pre-finished facings, then pour filler material into the interior of the wall. title: FLOOR-CEILING VAULTS
summary_en: Form floor slabs and ceilings into elliptical arches, with an arch rise equal to 13% to 20% of the shorter span. The adopted construction process allows arches to be fitted to rooms of any arbitrary shape after walls and columns are fully positioned, and prefabricated arches are not permitted for use under any circumstances. The resulting FLOOR-CEILING VAULTS are subject to two constraints: the ceiling at the room edge shall not be lower than approximately 6 feet (except for occasional attic rooms), while the ceiling at the room center shall be correspondingly higher.

summary_en: Under no circumstances should standard doors and windows be used. Each window shall have a distinct size corresponding to its specific location. summary_en: Construct a curved diagonal arch the same way you build the floor-slab ceiling vault (219). title: RADIANT HEAT
summary_en: Select a primarily radiant heating method for your spaces, especially rooms where people gather during cold weather, to ensure more heat is delivered via RADIANT HEAT rather than convection. title: ROOF CAPS
summary_en: Select a natural capping approach for the roof that is commensurate with the building's construction method and architectural connotation. title: LAPPED OUTSIDE WALLS
summary_en: The surface of LAPPED OUTSIDE WALLS is constructed using layers of mutually lapped materials to resist wind and rain, which follows two implementation modes: (1) "internal lapping" represented by exterior wall plastering, and (2) direct lapping represented by wood shingles, planks and tiles. All such applications select materials that are easy to repair in small units at low cost, so that the wall surface can be incrementally and indefinitely maintained in good condition.

numbers_en.k: Construct exterior wall surface with layers of mutually lapped wind and rain resistant materials

Select materials that are easy to repair in small sections at low cost, to perpetually maintain the wall in good condition

title: SOFT INSIDE WALLS
summary_en: One excellent material is soft white gypsum plaster. It has a warm hue even in its white form, delivers a mild warm tactile feel, is soft enough to accept thumbtacks, nails and hooks directly, is easy to repair, and produces a mellow, full sound due to its considerably high sound absorption capacity. Cement plaster, by contrast, is only marginally different and often confused with gypsum plaster, but has completely opposite performance in all these aspects: it is far too hard to drive fasteners into comfortably, and presents a cold, rigid tactile experience.

numbers_en.v: Soft white gypsum plaster is optimal
numbers_en.k: Soft white gypsum plaster: warm color, warm tactile feel, soft enough to hold thumbtacks, nails and hooks, easy to repair, mellow acoustic performance
Avoid cold, rigid cement plaster that cannot be comfortably penetrated by fasteners

title: WINDOWS WHICH OPEN WIDE
summary_en: In modern design, permanently sealed windows paired with mechanical air conditioning to create a "perfect" indoor climate are becoming a widespread, irrational default. Windows serve as the critical connection between occupants and the external environment: they are the source of fresh air, a simple measure to rapidly adjust indoor temperatures when rooms are overheated or overly cold, and a space for people to lean out and smell the surrounding outdoor air. Adopt the WINDOWS WHICH OPEN WIDE specification: design operable windows as side-hinged casement windows that swing fully outward, and reject sealed picture windows and sliding sash windows that only open to 50% of their total opening area.

title: SOLID DOORS WITH GLASS
summary_en: Wherever possible, adopt SOLID DOORS WITH GLASS, with at least the upper half of each door transparent to allow unobstructed views through. Make the door sufficiently thick to deliver effective sound insulation, and emit a satisfying solid thud when fully closed. This door type achieves both partial visual connection between adjacent spaces and the quiet, enclosed tranquility when the door is shut.

title: FILTERED LIGHT
summary_en: At all locations where window edges or overhanging roof eaves form silhouettes against the sky, a rich, finely woven chiaroscuro tapestry is created to fragment incident light and soften it. The FILTERED LIGHT effect generated when light filters through a lush, heavily foliated tree is widely recognized as highly pleasant, bringing excitement, brightness and joy, while uniform, unmodulated illumination produces dull, uninspiring spaces.

title: SMALL PANES
summary_en: Full unbroken large clear glass windows would seemingly draw nature closer to people, as they appear more like an opening, nearly indistinguishable from open air. In fact, however, these large panes instead alienate people from the exterior view. The smaller the window and the smaller the individual SMALL PANES, the more strongly the window connects occupants to the elements on its opposite side. Accordingly, every window is divided into multiple small panes using glass muntins.

numbers_en.k: Divide every window into multiple small panes using glass muntins

title: HALF-INCH TRIM
summary_en: At every junction where two different materials meet, a trim strip is mounted to cover the edge of the seam. Following the HALF-INCH TRIM specification, the narrowest strip within each component assembly is consistently selected to be roughly half an inch wide, with acceptable trim materials including wood, gypsum, and terracotta. A free, naturally conceived building is unimaginable without the use of such trim strips to finish edges and conceal all minor deviations generated during planar design and on-site construction.

title: SEAT SPOTS
summary_en: Selecting optimal locations for outdoor seating is far more critical than constructing ornate decorative benches. Indeed, as long as placement is appropriate, even the simplest type of seat is a perfect SEAT SPOT. In cool climates, position seats to face the sun and avoid wind exposure; in hot climates, place them in shaded areas that catch summer breezes. Under all circumstances, orient the seats to face adjacent active areas.

numbers_en.k: Selecting good locations for outdoor seating is far more important than building fancy benches

title: FRONT DOOR BENCH
summary_en: Place a dedicated FRONT DOOR BENCH outside the front door, so that residents inside the dwelling can sit comfortably for hours watching the surrounding street life pass by. The placement of this bench effectively demarcates a distinct semi-private territory in the front setback of the home. A low wall, a planting patch, or a single tree can all help generate this same semi-private domain. People do not always desire unmediated, full engagement with the public street: casual lingering requires a continuous spectrum of varying levels of connection to the public street realm.

numbers_en.k: Place a dedicated FRONT DOOR BENCH outside the front door to support extended relaxed sitting while observing passing street activity

title: SITTING WALL
summary_en: Use SITTING WALLS that are approximately 16 inches high and wide enough for seating (at least 12 inches in width) to enclose any natural outdoor site, and delineate subtle boundaries between different outdoor spaces. Take a garden adjacent to a quiet street as an example: along the boundary between the two, a seam is required at no fewer than one location — a spot that connects the two spaces, while not erasing the fact that they are two distinct, independent places.

title: CANVAS ROOFS
summary_en: For any space that requires softer light or partial shade in summer, or protection from mist and dew in autumn and winter, set up CANVAS ROOFS, walls and awnings. These elements are designed to be foldable and retractable, fitted with ropes or steel wires for operation to enable easy opening and closing. In conventional construction practice, people often assume walls and roofs must be either solid or completely absent; fabric and canvas occupy the exact intermediate state between these two extremes, as they are semi-translucent and allow a small amount of light to pass through.

title: RAISED FLOWERS
summary_en: Elevate flower beds with low supporting walls to bring blooms to a height where people do not need to bend over to reach out and touch the flowers, or lean in to inhale their scent, softening the hard edges between buildings, roads and outdoor seating spaces. Structures planted with roses, vines or honeysuckle hold far greater significance for people than buildings with bare, blank facades. By positioning the RAISED FLOWERS at arm's reach and face level, this intimate proximity to flowering greenery is made readily accessible.

title: CLIMBING PLANTS
summary_en: On sun-facing walls, guide CLIMBING PLANTS to twine and grow along all openings on the wall, including windows, doors, porticos, arcades, and trellises. There is no doubt that a building with climbing roses, vines or honeysuckle growing on its facade holds far more significance for people than a building with bare, blank exterior walls. This rationale alone is sufficient to justify planting wild clematis outside buildings and installing planter boxes to support climbing vegetation to grow to greater heights.

title: PAVING WITH CRACKS BETWEEN THE STONES
summary_en: Implement the PAVING WITH CRACKS BETWEEN THE STONES technique on walkways and patios, leaving 1-inch gaps between stones to allow grass, moss, and small flowering plants to grow through the joints. Set the paving stones directly into soil rather than a mortar bed, and never use cement or mortar to fill the gaps between stones. This unpretentious walkway, built by laying bricks or paving stones directly into the earth with wide open joints, carries a uniquely warm and approachable quality.

title: SOFT TILE AND BRICK
summary_en: SOFT TILE AND BRICK are produced via soft, low-temperature firing, so that they wear gradually over time and reveal clear traces of use. You can source local clay on site to form unfired raw units in a simple mold, then surround the stacked raw units with kindling and firewood for firing to achieve a gentle pink hue. Bricks fired through this process are soft enough to naturally develop distinct wear marks as they are put to use.

title: ORNAMENT
summary_en: Circulate around the building to locate edges and transitions that require emphasis or an additional binding force. Corners, material joints, door frames, windows, main entrances, wall-to-wall junctions, garden gates, and fences are all sites that naturally call for ORNAMENT. Applying ORNAMENT at these locations binds and integrates the two sides of the joint into a unified whole.

title: WARM COLORS
summary_en: Select surface colors that, together with the color tones of natural light, reflected light, and artificial light, produce a warm luminous field inside the room. Broadly speaking, under the WARM COLORS framework, red, yellow, orange, and brown are categorized as warm hues, while blue, green, and gray are categorized as cool hues. This classification is not absolute, and the core criterion is whether the combination of these colors and all ambient light immerses the entire room in a soft, warm luminous environment.

title: DIFFERENT CHAIRS
summary_en: Never furnish any space using exactly identical chairs. Curate a diverse collection of DIFFERENT CHAIRS: varying in size, with some softer than others, including rocking chairs, heavily worn old pieces, brand new models, armchairs, armless chairs, and options constructed from rattan, wood, or upholstered in fabric. While fully uniform chair sets are typically driven by prefabrication-related requirements, people are inherently distinct from one another, so appropriate seating should logically differ accordingly.

title: POOLS OF LIGHT
summary_en: Place luminaires at a low elevation and space them apart from one another, so each forms a distinct POOLS OF LIGHT that wraps around chairs and tables like a bubble, reinforcing the social attribute of the enclosed spaces they demarcate. Keep in mind that POOLS OF LIGHT can never be achieved without the relatively dim intermediate zones between them. The egg-crate ceiling typology, densely fitted with evenly spaced rows of fluorescent lights that intentionally produce flat, uniform illumination, is a misguided effort intended to mimic the natural sky.

title: THINGS FROM YOUR LIFE
summary_en: Don’t be misled into assuming modern interior decoration must be sleek, psychedelic, "natural", "modern art", full of green foliage, or aligned with any other aesthetic promoted by today’s taste-makers. Decoration reaches its highest beauty when it originates directly from THINGS FROM YOUR LIFE: the possessions you treasure, the objects that narrate your personal story. This plain fact can be viewed from two perspectives: the perspective of the person who owns the space, and the perspective of the person who enters the space.
